speechtext: Shall the Hon. Member have leave to introduce the Bill?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to sponsor today a Bill which is entitled "An Act to amend the National Defence Act". The purpose of the Bill is to amend the National Defence Act in order to remove all references to the death penalty for offences committed under the Act. A sentence of life imprisonment would replace all references to the death penalty.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, in 1976 this Parliament abolished the death penalty as far as the Criminal Code of Canada was concerned. The death penalty continues to exist in the National Defence Act and, as I indicated, the purpose of this Bill is to make the National Defence Act consistent with the Criminal Code of Canada. Capital punishment is wrong, whether it is in the Criminal Code of Canada or in the National Defence Act. Capital punishment is morally wrong whether it is done by hanging or by firing squad under the provisions of the National Defence Act.
Capital punishment is the mark of an indecent, uncivilized and immoral society. I regret very much that the Government is embarking upon a very divisive and emotionally charged debate on the issue of capital punishment with regard to the Criminal Code of Canada.
In closing I wish to indicate that the last time an individual was executed under the provisions of the National Defence Act was in 1945 during the Second World War. In the First World War 26 Canadian soldiers were executed by a firing squad for breaches of the provisions of the National Defence Act. This Bill will eliminate that possibility in future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I gave notice of a point of order on Friday which I wish to pursue now. I did not feel it was appropriate to pursue it on Friday since it was a Liberal opposition day. This point of order specifically deals with the practice of the New Democratic Party during this session with respect to petitions. Petitions are being certified by the Clerk of Petitions and then formally presented in the House of Commons some weeks or months later as part of a deliberate practice on the part of the New Democratic Party.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that on Tuesday, March 17, 1987, I requested the data of certification of a petition being submitted by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). He replied that the petition in question had been certified on October 1, 1986. That would be some five months earlier. On March 19, I asked the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) as to the date of the certification of a petition presented on March 19. It was certified on January 6 of this year. Both of these petitions, I might add, were with respect to the Patent Act changes.
March 23, 1987

If the Chair were to review Petition No. 332-1271, the Chair would find it was approved on June 12, 1986, and presented on March 9, 1987. If the Chair were to review Petition No. 3321276, presented by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) with respect to the Patent Act, the Chair would find it was approved on November 7, 1986, and presented on March 10, 1987.
This practice is continuing. In fact, on Friday, March 20, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) presented three petitions. The petitioners were supposed to be very concerned about the Patent Act changes. Those three petitions were certified by the Clerk of Petitions on November 26, 1986, four months earlier, and then presented last Friday. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that members of the New Democratic Party are bringing the House into disrepute by this abuse of one of the fundamental principles of our democratic system for blatant political purposes.
Citation 666 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, states:
The right of petitioning the Crown and Parliament for redress of grievances is
acknowledged as a fundamental principle of the constitution and has been
exercised without interruption since 1867.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that by certifying petitions and holding them for formal presentation in the House on a daily basis, the New Democratic Party seeks to create the impression that there is a continuing ground swell of public opinion with respect to a certain issue which is continuing for a long period of time. I submit this is an abuse of a longstanding parliamentary tradition. This abuse denies Canadians who have petitioned the Crown and Parliament for redress of their grievances speedy access to that redress. It brings Parliament into disrepute. It unfairly creates the impression of a long-standing issue and denies the Government of the day the right to reply promptly either to the petition or to the individuals who signed the petition.
You will know from the former occupation you and I both share, Mr. Speaker, that there is an expression that justice delayed is justice denied. Canadians who petition the Crown and Government have every right to expect that the Crown will receive their petitions quickly if they entrust them to a Member of Parliament and that the Crown will take the petitions into account. If a Member of Parliament has a petition certified and then delays the presentation of that petition for political purposes, that hearing and redress are unfairly delayed.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that Members of Parliament have a responsibility to present petitions as soon as possible after certification. If they cannot do it in person, there is a practice in the rules of procedure whereby the petition can be filed with the Table and have the same force and effect. I suggest that this practice brings Parliament into disrepute. The distortion of the petition process brings this entire Chamber and its Members into disrepute.
I have no difficulty whatsoever with the formal presentation of petitions. That is part of our tradition and should continue. However, Canadians who signed these petitions trust their
Point of Order-Mr. Lewis
Members of Parliament to present them promptly. If they are delayed for political purposes, then I suggest that Canadians are going to view the petition process with great skepticism. I suggest that petitions are a legitimate gauge of public opinion if they are fairly worded and presented promptly. While the delay in the presentation of a petition does not diminish how the signatories feel about the issue, if they are delayed in order to create the impression of a long-standing grievance, then that distorts the situation.
Your Honour will also know that under Standing Order 106(8) the Government is required to reply to a petition within 45 days. Today I tabled some 83 replies of the Government. We have respected that deadline. We have also gone further and in some cases written to individual petitioners.
I have here for examination, if Your Honour cares to review it, a letter which is being sent to all petitioners in the case of the Patent Act by the Hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), in which he states very fully the Government's case in respect of changes to the Patent Act.
While I would not suggest that the petitions are being tampered with, I would suggest that there are examples of letters in reply which read as follows: "I never corresponded with anybody on this subject and I have no interest in the matter"; "I suspect that somebody has wrongly used my name for political purposes"; "The reason for my mystification is that I have never corresponded with the Prime Minister on this or any other subject"; and "I have never written to you concerning the hassle over generic drugs, nor have I signed any petition". I do not want to pursue that aspect of this point of order any further. I just raise the question.
The second abuse of the petition process is that Members of Parliament from the New Democratic Party are misleading Parliament when they present petitions certified by other members in a deliberate attempt to create the impression that an issue has widespread concern.
On Friday, March 20, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) distributed petitions to his colleagues in the NDP for presentation in the House. The Hon. Member for Yorkton- Melville (Mr. Nystrom), the Hon. Member for Humboldt- Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), and the Hon. Member for Cowichan- Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) participated in this charade. All those petitions-and I have them here-were certified by the Hon. Member for Spadina on Thursday, March 19. On Friday, the Hon. Member came into the House and distributed them to his colleagues for presentation. All the addresses on those petitions were from Metropolitan Toronto and area.
By having these petitions presented by Members from Saskatchewan and British Columbia, the Hon. Member for Spadina sought to have Parliament believe that Canadians in different parts of the country were petitioning Parliament for

March 23, 1987
Point of Order-Mr. Lewis
redress. If that is not deliberately misleading the House, it comes as close to deliberately misleading the House as anything in my experience.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 heard very carefully the words of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, which were "if that is not deliberately misleading the House", it comes very close to it. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is also as close to getting out of order as he can be. I will take account of the very careful wording he used, but I would ask that he be extremely careful as he continues his remarks.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I take your admonition.
As I said earlier, we have no difficulty with the legitimate presentation of petitions. However, I would point out that in the month of February an hour and a half of the time of the House was spent on the presentation of petitions. Since the opening of this Parliament on October 1, almost seven hours of House time have been given to this procedure. The Hon. House Leader of the New Democratic Party can hardly complain about the lack of time for debate when we find that it is being wasted in this manner.
I suggest that the delaying of the presentation of petitions in order to pretend that a long-standing issue exists is a cheap political trick. It is a complete fabrication and a charade. It is an attempt to mislead the House and the Canadian public.
1 further suggest that the practice of distributing petitions to other MPs by the member who certified them, in order to pretend that there is an issue of widespread concern, is also a cheap political trick, a complete fabrication and charade, and an attempt to mislead the House and the Canadian public.
The holier than thou New Democratic Party will stop at nothing for partisan political purposes. The rights of petitioners mean nothing to them. The rights of Parliament mean nothing to them. The reputation of their fellow Members of Parliament who present petitions are completely disregarded. I call upon the Chair to examine this practice and to stop what I consider to be a complete abuse of the House.
I suggest the Chair rule that in the future petitions must be presented in a timely fashion by the Member of Parliament who certified them. In the alternative, I suggest that Your Honour might want the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure to review the matter to safeguard the rights of petitioners to timely presentation of their petitions to the Crown and Parliament, rather than subject them to cheap partisan political tactics by members of the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, in summing up, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader said that since October 1 members of all three Parties have used a total of seven hours to present petitions. He has made it sound like they have taken a large amount of time. If the Government were so concerned about the amount of time it needs for government business, it could have called the House
back in September. Seven hours over as many months is not a large proportion of time. I do not think the Parliamentary Secretary has a legitimate point in that area.
Opposition Members have complaints with regard to the Government, and I should like to refer to one example. Sometimes we wait a very long time to get answers from the Parliamentary Secretary to questions we have placed on the Order Paper. Yet, we have avoided the tactic of getting up every day and asking when a question will be answered. We have not wasted House time on that. It is a legitimate right of opposition Members to rise and ask when the Parliamentary Secretary will finally answer a particular question.
With regard to the substance of the matter raised by the Parliamentary Secretary, and in that he mentioned that I have risen on a number of occasions, in my particular case one of my petitions was certified in January and it took me approximately two months to present it. He should also realize that I have had from a very small population riding over a thousand people who have written on this particular item. They do not come on one piece of paper. They come in on pieces of paper with two or three names or five or ten names.
This means that it was not a petition which I circulated on November 1 and brought into the House on November 6. In truth, people are still writing in to me, signing petitions, and expressing their grievances with regard to the Government. If we used the Gallup polls, I would suspect that there is an increasing dissatisfaction with the Government over the passage of time. People who used to vote Conservative and are concerned about issues are people who are now supporting us and writing to us.
I understand the Government's concern that we do not present petitions right away. It is a legitimate concern of the Government. However, I think our petitioners would want us to make as effective a use of the presentation of petitions as possible. The people who sign petitions would understand if- and today I could have done so on behalf of Churchill, Pikwitonei, Flin Flon, and The Pas, Manitoba-I rose a week or two later, or perhaps even later, to present petitions on behalf of people in some of those same communities and in other communities expressing their particular grievance with the Government.
In the case of the patent drug legislation, over 1,200 people from my riding alone have signed petitions. They did so on November 6, December 15 and in January. Obviously some people are still signing petitions today and I will continue to present them in the House. This issue is still before the House. Legislation will soon be studied at report stage and then we will have third reading. It is an active issue and an issue on which we have a right to present petitions.
[DOT] (U30)
The other matter raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lewis) has to do with the habit, practised by some members, of circulating petitions.
March 23, 1987

If a petition is received by one member, he or she takes on the responsibility of having it certified but may ask another Member to present it in the House. I have taken part in that process, Mr. Speaker, and I consider that honourable. I have taken petitions that do not come from my riding but come from New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, places where we do not have New Democratic Members of Parliament at present-
Spadina?

I have had them certified. I believe people send petitions to the New Democratic Party wanting their petitions raised in the House of Commons. It matters not to them whether it is the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), Brant (Mr. Blackburn), Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) or Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) that presents the petition. The petitions were not sent to me as an individual but to our caucus and people expect a member of our caucus to present them.
I have looked at Beauchesne and our Standing Orders since the Parliamentary Secretary indicated his concern on this issue, and I thank him for giving notice of it. I see nothing in the rules to say that the same Member who received a petition, often from people in other ridings, must have it certified and that he or she must present it in the House. It may seem cleaner or more efficient, but if I receive a petition, as I used the example before, from people in New Brunswick and I have received it because it came into my office as caucus whip, I do not feel it is my obligation to present that petition in the House. I will, however, get it certified so that it is ready to be presented and I will make sure it is given to the Clerk of Petitions. It may be appropriate when the time comes for some other Member to present the petition, perhaps someone who has been in the locale in the last little while or perhaps someone whose critic area is more directly concerned with the topic being presented.
It seems to me the Government is concerned that we are making this a political issue, that by holding off petitions and not presenting them all on the date they are certified, by presenting them over a number of days or in the case of having a number of petitions presented on the same day by a number of people, that this is political. God help us, Mr. Speaker, if we are ever political in the House of Commons. How dreadful it would be if we tried to make a Government Bill into a political issue that would not be within the rules of the House of Commons. God help us, Mr. Speaker, if we have the situation with the Government not liking a petition and harassing us day after day in one fashion or another. We had the spectre last fall of the Government House Leader (Mr. Mazankowski) wanting to see our petitions before we presented them. He found that they were in the proper form and we were allowed to continue presenting them.
In the last couple of weeks the Parliamentary Secretary to the House Leader saw the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) pass a petition to the Hon. Member for
Point of Order-Mr. Lewis
Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly). The Parliamentary Secretary rose and said that that was not fair, that the petition obviously belonged to the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap. Unfortunately for the Parliamentary Secretary someone had asked the Member from Kamloops-Shuswap to give the petition to the Member for Comox-Powell River because the petitioners were from the riding of Comox- Powell River. This again was part of a pattern of harassment by the Government. To be fair to the Parliamentary Secretary, he did apologize on that occasion.
I do not think the point of order that has been raised today is legitimate. It may be something that concerns the Government in its political role. But if we have had only seven hours taken up by petitions since October, some of which have been presented by Government Members and some by Liberal Members, I would say that some Government Members are not doing their jobs. Lots of people would like members to present petitions. Obviously we are not spending very much time in the House with legitimate complaints, beefs and concerns of people who live in Government ridings.
With respect, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that this is a serious issue. The Government is in a situation to know when petitions are certified. The Government is in the position, as the Parliamentary Secretary has said, of responding on an individual basis to petitions. The Government may not like our political agenda, but we do not like the Government's either.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on listening to the point of order raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lewis) and to the reply by the spokesman for the New Democratic Party, I was at first tempted to allow this matter to pass by as just another indication of the ongoing battle between the Conservatives and New Democrats for third place. However, after reflecting somewhat on the arguments presented, I think there is a point here about which comment has to be made.
It is a matter of concern that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council finds it necessary on a day when there is an Opposition motion before the House to raise this point of order and to ask the Speaker to take it seriously. The Parliamentary Secretary said that you should rule that petitions can only be presented to this House immediately by those who have received them and who have had them certified. I invite you to look at the rules of order of this House, Mr. Speaker, Standing Order 106(3) which reads:
A petition to the House may be presented by a Member at any time during the
sitting of the House by filing the same with the Clerk of the House.
I draw your attention to some of the words "may be presented by a member at any time during the sitting of the House". Also, if you look at Standing Order 106(4), it reads:
Any Member desiring to present a petition, in his or her place in the House,
may do so on "Presenting Petitions" during the ordinary daily routine of
business.
Nowhere in the very precise language used by the Standing Order does it say that a petition has to be presented to this

March 23, 1987
Point of Order-Mr. Lewis
House as soon as it is received by a Member. Nowhere does it say that the member who presents the petition has to be the one who receives it in the first instance. I think it is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that you do not have the authority to make a ruling which clashes with the clear words of the Standing Orders of this House.
Some months ago when members attempted to present to the House all the petitions they had received on a subject on the same day, Government spokesmen got to their feet and raised a point of order saying that this was of questionable validity because it unduly ate up the time of the House that otherwise would be available for Government business and other proceedings. Today, however, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader is saying that there is something wrong if instead of trying to present all your petitions on the same day you do a few at a time so as to take up less time on any particular day.
Just what is the Government after? I hate to suggest this, but I wonder if the Government is not trying to choke off an elementary right of Canadians and an elementary right of opposition Parties on their behalf to petition Government through Parliament. Why else would the Deputy House Leader raise this rather strange point of order which flies in the face of the clear language of the Standing Orders and also flies in the face of the position taken by the Government months ago when members attempted to present petitions to the House as soon as they were received, no matter how much time it took on any particular day? The Hon. Member cannot have it both ways. I say that Hon. Members do not have to do this, but if the Deputy House Leader wants members to present petitions as soon as they receive them, the Government cannot complain about the time being taken up on any particular day when time is being used for that purpose.
The Deputy House Leader for the Government is saying that somehow or other, people who present petitions to the House through Members of Parliament are aggrieved if those petitions are not presented very soon after they are signed and sent here. Quite apart from the fact that the Standing Orders do not require that this approach be taken, if there is any complaint about when a petition is presented, it is a complaint of the person or persons signing the petition, not of the Government to whom that petition is addressed. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader certainly has no mandate to raise this point allegedly on behalf of those presenting petitions. As I have said, the complaint, if there is any complaint, is solely that of those who have signed the petition.
It might be argued that the rules also indicate that members can simply table petitions and file them with the Clerk, but that is an option to be used at the discretion of the member who wishes to present the petition. It is not something that can be imposed upon any member by the Government. To suggest that, is a total distortion of what the rules say and a total distortion of the right of petitioning Parliament. It is certainly
a total distortion of the role of Government and Opposition in a democratic Parliament.
I have said before that since members of the present Government came into office they have through various means attempted to operate as if this were some type of one-Party state. That was not the case after the election and it is not the case now. Certainly this is confirmed every day by public opinion polls. It is not proper for the Government to try to tell members that, rather than using their own judgment or the judgment of those signing petitions about presenting petitions in open sessions of the House, they must instead file them with the Clerk. That is the choice primarily of the Member of Parliament who wishes to present the petition.
The Parliamentary Secretary has complained that since last fall seven hours have allegedly been used for presenting petitions. As has been pointed out, this is not a lot of time compared to the total number of sitting hours since then. But what concerns me is that he implied that using this time to present petitions is somehow wasting the time of the House. Yet, at the beginning of his remarks, he was ready to admit that one of the most fundamental rights of people in Canada is the right to petition the Government through Parliament about their concerns. It cannot be both a waste of time and a fundamental right to be exercised according to our rules.
I conclude by saying that not only do the rules clearly permit what the Hon. Member is complaining of, but also that if you accept as well founded the point of order of the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, the result will be to choke off the rights of Canadians to petition the Government and the rights of opposition Members to speak on behalf of people who wish to petition the Government.
Why is the member who is speaking on behalf of the Government so sensitive about this issue at this time? One can only conclude that government Members fear the voices of the Canadian people. They want to choke off the voices of ordinary Canadians. We in the Official Opposition do not intend to let them do that. We want to make sure that those voices can be heard through petitions and through Members of Parliament until the time comes when the voices of Canadians are heard during an election and this thoroughly bad Government is thrown out of office.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few comments because the matter is of some interest to me. As Hon. Members are aware, I am one of those members who present a considerable number of petitions in this House, petitions that are often taken up by people in my riding. I will not name the various subjects they deal with, but I think a look at the record will show that I have presented petitions on many occasions.
Mr. Speaker, to find a statement on the right of petitioning, we must refer to Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Beau-chesne's 5th edition.
March 23, 1987

The right of petitioning the Crown and Parliament for redress of grievances is acknowledged as a fundamental principle of the constitution and has been exercised without interruption since 1867.
I am referring to Citation 666, on page 209, In fact, while my colleagues were speaking, I read a little further and something caught my eye. There are a number of details concerning who may present a petition and how one is to proceed. After discussing remonstrances, signatures and the substance of the petition, Beauchesne raises a question that deals precisely with the point raised by the Hon. Member, namely that if we have a petition prepared in the riding and we present it in the House, is there any provision in the Standing Orders that obliges us to do so with celerity, in other words, as soon as possible, and is it mandatory that petitions taken up in our ridings for any number of reasons be presented by the member for the riding in which they were taken up?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise two points which I think are of some interest and I will start with Citation 689 on page 212 in Beauchesne's, appearing under the title:

689.	As the Speaker does not take part in debates, and may be called to give decisions on the regularity of petitions, he does not present petitions to the House. When asked by his constituents to do so, he must avail himself of the services of another Member-
There is a reference to Bourinot, page 231, and May, page 817. And reading further:
690.	A member may petition the House but his petition should be presented by another Member-
In other words, I may be included among the petitioners, but in that case another Member has to present the petition for me.
This deals with the objection raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council, namely that the Standing Orders, and I am referring to Standing Order 106(4), do not indicate it must be the same member. I may be another member, and all the NDP Members have to do, if they are accused of "packing in" petitions will be to sign the petitions and say: I am not qualified because I signed the petition so would you present the petition for me.

Except for very clear dispositions adopted on February 24, 1986, to get rid of a lot of grey areas, there is nothing in the Standing Orders to state that a member is limited to presenting only petitions that he has gathered or, for that matter, petitions that he has had certified. I have taken perhaps 35 or 40 petitions to the Clerk of Petitions on one morning. It was physically impossible for her to certify all those petitions that day because there were a great many others to be certified. I was patient and waited for her to call back. When the petitions came in we tabled them as fast as we could. However, it was sometimes impossible for me to table all the petitions on the same day because of some difficulty in getting them certified, and at other times because of their great number.
Point of Order-Mr. Lewis
What happens when a member is absent? Is the Parliamentary Secretary telling us that when a petition is presented as certified this day, it must be presented, in his words, immediately or in a timely fashion? Does that mean they have to be tabled that day? I think that would be difficult for some members who have things to do other than be sitting in this House. They have committee work or they may be outside the House doing other parliamentary work. It would be kind of difficult to demand that members table the petition on the day it was certified.
The Government must now present a reply to the petition within 45 days, and that is good. However, the Government's argument concerning time is superfluous and possibly not very timely because the Government wastes more time than anyone else in telling us very little about its legislation. As a matter of fact, many Canadians anticipate government legislation and present their petitions to us before the legislation is brought in. This happens even to government Members. On the list of petitions answered today by the Government there is one from a government Member. He could have received that petition from his constituents or from others within his sphere of interest. It does happen that groups of people, not necessarily from one riding, petition Parliament, as is their right. For example, God knows, we have presented several petitions here from senior citizens and they were not always from the riding of Ottawa-Vanier. They may have been from Ottawa Centre, Ottawa-Carleton, or anywhere else. The argument that a member must table a petition in a timely fashion is fine as long as we accept that the Member is not obligated to table only petitions from his riding. Mind you, the person tabling the petition must sign it. I do not think it would be proper for a Member of this House to table a petition signed by another member. That is wrong. If you asked me to table a petition in your name, Mr. Speaker, I would sign it but it would be constituents of yours who want to petition the House over a grievance in an attempt to rectify a situation about which they feel strongly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have listened very carefully to what was said by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) and the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), and of course to the intervention by the Parliamentary Secretary.

I think there is one essential issue emerging from the exchange, that perhaps there is some concern that when a citizen signs a petition he perhaps ought to know how much time elapses from the time he signed the petition to the time it is presented in the House. That presentation triggers the obligation on the part of the Government to reply within 45 days. That is a matter which the Chair will consider.
I will look with some care at the documentation and procedure and I may be able to make some comment which is

March 23, 1987
Supply
helpful at a later time. Certainly the right to present petitions is an undoubted right of a free people. It is our constitutional tradition. I did not take anything said today, intentionally anyway, to be a suggestion that that right ought to be infringed. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier pointed out that there is an obligation upon the Chair to ask another Hon. Member to present petitions presented to me. I should advise Hon. Members that I do receive petitions regularly and I have to ask the indulgence of other Hon. Members to present them.
I think the essential thing coming out of this debate is that people who sign petitions have a fair certainty that the Government is responding with due diligence as soon as possible after the petition is received. Perhaps the Chair can assist Hon. Members by examining the response the Government makes in its reply to petitions within 45 days of the petition coming to the attention of the House, as it is obligated to do.
For Hon. Members who may not be as fully aware of past practices, and also for the benefit of the public who is watching and listening, it should be pointed out that the obligation on the Government to reply to petitions within 45 days is part of parliamentary reform. While there certainly was an ancient and undoubted right to present petitions, there was no corresponding obligation on the part of the Government to respond to them.
I find that the interventions are of interest. I can assure all Hon. Members that the Chair will be diligent at all times to ensure that any Canadian who presents a petition to this Chamber will have every opportunity to have it responded to by the Government. I will consider some of the paperwork and address the question of whether or not a citizen may be under the apprehension that the Government is not replying rapidly enough to a petition which may have been signed many weeks or months previously. I think that is probably a matter that can properly be discussed.
I thank all Hon. Members, including the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Windsor West, the Hon. Member for Churchill, and of course the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
In fact, from January, 1986, to January, 1987, only 5,000 of the 137,000 jobs created in Canada were created outside of Ontario. I am glad that the economy of southern Ontario is doing well, but there is a real problem of unemployment in northern Ontario, Quebec, the Atlantic Provinces and western Canada.
In my part of the country the situation is now much worse than it was in the 1970s or in the early 1980s. In February the unemployment rate in British Columbia was 13.4 per cent, in Alberta it was 10.9 per cent, in Saskatchewan it was 7.2 per cent, and in Manitoba it was 6.7 per cent.
Those figures tell only part of the story. Looking at regional unemployment rates in Canada we see that many parts of the west have unemployment rates which are exceptionally high. In the Kamloops, British Columbia, area the unemployment rate is 19.1 per cent; in the Kimberley-Cranbrook area it is 17.4 per cent; in the City of Edmonton and area it is 12.8 per cent; in the City of Vancouver it is 14.2 per cent, in northern Saskatchewan it is over 10 per cent; in the City of Saskatoon it is 10.4 per cent; in the City of Winnipeg it is about 7.8 per cent; and in Dauphin and northern Manitoba it is about 9.3 per cent. Therefore, in many parts of western Canada there are extremely high unemployment rates. That, Madam Speaker, is not good enough.
What has that done to western Canadians? What has that done to hospital boards, municipalities, and school boards? When I go to my riding every couple of weeks I see nothing but concern and despair about the future economy of western Canada. I find that all four western provinces are having serious economic problems. Deficits are being run up. Provincial governments are being forced to increase the taxes of the citizens of the provinces. In my Province of Saskatchewan the matching grants of two municipalities have been frozen for two years. There will be increases in the mill rates in municipal taxes. The costs of school boards and hospitals will be passed on to local municipalities.
A new Budget was recently brought down in British Columbia with major tax increases for British Columbians. There is a tremendous deficit in Alberta for the first time in many years. A new Budget was brought in there with major increases in taxation for Albertans. There are economic problems in terms of a deficit in Manitoba and massive economic problems in terms of a deficit in Saskatchewan.
I would like to spend a minute speaking about my own province because that is the one I know best. I would like to draw to the attention of the House something which I think is scandalous in a province of only one million people, that is, that we have a deficit in our province this year of $1.2 billion. A province with one million people has a deficit of $1.2 billion. I have a chart which shows that in 1983 the deficit was $227 million, in 1984 it was $331 million, in 1985 it was $395 million, in 1986 it was $584 million, and in 1987 the deficit in Saskatchewan is $1.2 billion. All throughout the 1940s, 1950s, 1960s and 1970s Saskatchewan had a surplus and a balanced Budget, almost all the time. Under the governments of Tommy
Supply
Douglas, Woodroffe Lloyd, Ross Thatcher and Allan Blakeney we did not have deficits in Saskatchewan. Although it is not entirely the fault of Grant Devine, we now have a deficit for which future generations will have to pay. It is massive, indeed.
I would like to refer to one or two sentences from an article in the business section of the Leader Post which talks about the massive deficit back home. It states that this deficit is three times larger than predicted by the Minister of Finance in his last Budget. That shows the severity of the problem facing western Canadians. The article goes on to state that it marks the fifth time in as many years the Progressive Conservative Government has missed its deficit target. This time the deficit has taken a quantum leap into the stratosphere. That is from the business pages of the Regina Leader Post of Friday, March 6.
We have very serious economic problems right across western Canada. I will speak about the farm economy and the energy economy later. I think we are all quite aware of what are some of those problems. My colleague, the Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) will be speaking about forestry this afternoon.
What is the Government's record with regard to western Canada? In the last Budget we saw the continuation of a cut of $3 billion a year from regional economic development spending in Canada. I noticed a Canadian Press article in the Toronto Sun this morning which said that the industry Minister has given strong indications that major changes including cut-backs are coming in the way the federal Government dispenses regional assistance. I would like the Minister to tell us in the House today what his plans are for regional development. This sends fear through the hearts of western Canadians who are already suffering from previous cut-backs and problems in the world economy which affect resources, agriculture, and other economic problems of western Canada.
Another problem is the insensitive way in which the Government is treating some western issues. I need only remind the House of the controversy in Manitoba over the CF-18 contract which was not awarded to the City of Winnipeg.
With regard to agriculture, the Government speaks of the $1 billion for grain farmers. I want to remind the House that even with the $1 billion our farmers get a lot less than the American and European farmers because of support prices in those countries. The farmers need more assistance as well if they are going to survive in western Canada.
The history of western Canada shows that there have been many grievances about the way the country has developed. One of those grievances concerns western Canada as a source of raw materials which are shipped to central Canada and other parts of the world with very little processing and development. The transportation system has discriminated against development in western Canada. These grievances and

March 23, 1987
Supply
others have existed for many years, but people thought they might be very positively addressed after September, 1984.
In the past, federal Governments have been insensitive to the problems of western Canada. The Liberal Party was almost decimated in western Canada for some 20 years because of its insensitivity to the problems of the West. We have seen the development of the CCF and the NDP, the Social Credit Party and other parties in the west because of the failure of federal governments to address western Canadian problems. That failure continues today.
One of my concerns is that once again in western Canada there are some signals that certain people are turning, in frustration, to western separatist groups like Western Canada Concept and the Confederation of Regions Party. One need only look at the riding of Lisgar in southern Manitoba and areas like that to see what I mean. I do not want to exaggerate that sentiment, but only want to point out that if we do not address some legitimate concerns soon more and more western Canadians will be extremely frustrated with the system.
I want to suggest a number of steps that we should be taking. The most important long-term step is to create a western economic development strategy that will have as its objective the diversification of the economy of western Canada. There have been many half-hearted attempts in the past to address that particular issue. I remember well the minority Parliament between 1972 and 1974 when Prime Minister Trudeau held a conference in Calgary called "WEOC", the Western Economic Opportunities Conference. There was great optimism again that a federal government, because of a minority Parliament, would perhaps listen to western Canada and do something substantive. In July, 1984, Mr. Trudeau was elected with a majority government and suddenly the priorities of western Canada were once again put on the back burner.
A few years later the Western Development Fund was announced. Once again there was a great deal of fanfare about this fund, but it never got off the ground and did nothing to help diversify the economy of western Canada. Although the Deputy Prime Minister has not announced this publicly, he has established with his colleagues a group in the City of Winnipeg to look at diversifying the economy of western Canada. This group was called the Western Initiatives Office in Winnipeg.

I have spoken to the people involved in the group, so I know of what I speak.
There should be a western economic development strategy. I know the Minister agrees with me in principle. Such a strategy should be based on three points. First, it should be based on
diversifying western Canada and building on the resource base and the agricultural base that already exist. I believe we can all agree that we have tremendous resources throughout the west, including great oil and gas resources in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Saskatchewan has immense potash reserves which represent about 30 per cent of the potash reserves in the world. There are tremendous forest resources throughout the Province of British Columbia and elsewhere in western Canada, and there are other resources in Manitoba and throughout the west. We need an economic strategy that will build on that particular foundation throughout western Canada and diversify the economy so there are jobs for western Canadians.
Second, we must build on agriculture in the west because of its great importance to our economy and the supply of food to the entire world.
Third, we need a change in transportation policy so that transportation will assist the western Canadian population rather than hinder it as it has done for so many years.
In addition to a western economic development strategy, I believe we must quickly take action to do more for agriculture if we want to save the family farm across the west. Let me put a couple of statistics on the record. We have heard about the real possibility of a drop in the initial price of wheat by some 20 per cent, after a drop in the price of wheat last year of about 19 per cent. If that happens, the price of wheat in this country for top quality grain will be some $2.83 a bushel. When one takes transportation to the Lakehead or the West Coast into account, top quality grains will produce some $2.37 a bushel. Let us compare that with the American farmer who receives $6.10 Canadian a bushel and the European farmer who receives $7 Canadian a bushel. How long can a farmer stay on the land at $2.37 a bushel in this country when the American farmer receives $6.10 and the European farmer receives $7? That is not good enough.
I have a study by the Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture which gives a breakdown of the cost of producing grain on a per acre basis. Again, the Department is talking about the impossibility of being able to even meet production costs in western Canada. The Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture says the farmer would have to produce an average of 58 bushels per acre of the top quality grain just to break even in the production of that grain, let alone meet the living costs of farmers and their families across western Canada today. When it comes to barley, it will be necessary to produce 135 bushels per acre if there is a drop of some 20 per cent in the price of barley, which everyone is predicting. Such production figures for the Prairies are absolutely unrealistic and impossible to meet. There are extremely serious problems in the grain economy, I suggest more serious than anything we saw in the 1930s. Farmers are receiving prices as low as $2.37 a bushel for the top quality grain and the price drops considerably for grades two, three, four and lower.
There are a number of ways to address the situation. First, we know that a major part of the problem is external because
March 23, 1987

we export most of our grain. The Government must continue to fight for an international grains agreement so that there is a pricing formula between the five major exporting and consuming nations of the world that is based on production costs of farmers around the world and the ability of consuming nations to pay.
Second, in the short term, we need another deficiency payment for western Canadian grain farmers. Even to guarantee last year's prices, we probably need a minimum of $2 billion for western Canadian grain farmers. It is incumbent on the House to come to the assistance of the farmers of the Prairies when they have a problem that is beyond their control, namely, the price wars and subsidy wars between the Americans and the European Economic Community. I believe we will have to give greater consideration to the necessity of providing a much greater deficiency payment than was provided last year.
We need a parity pricing system in which a farmer receives his cost of production and a decent profit for his products. We should be producing generic farm chemicals at cost in this country so that farmers can have chemicals at cost. The high price of fertilizer must be reduced in Canada to give farmers additional help.
Let me deal with energy. Our Party believes that there should be a floor price in energy so that there is a minimum price below which it will not be allowed to fall.

If we have strong partners in Confederation we will have a strong Canada. That will be good, not just for the West, but good for Ontario, Quebec, Atlantic and northern Canada as well.

Mr. Speaker, I am just delighted to have a chance to speak on the supply motion debate today because it really builds on the motion we put before the Elouse last Wednesday. On that day we saw Her Majesty's Government and back-benchers stand up and vote against our motion which called on the Government to make a commitment with regard to the agriculture situation in western Canada. We called upon the Government at that time to ensure that the returns for grain produced this coming year will be at least as good as they were in 1986-87, to maintain the freeze on freight rates in a new crop year, to take action to reduce farm input costs through the reduction in chemical prices, such as generic chemicals, and generally deal with the farm debt crisis. I would like to go into that in some detail today. All 125 government back-benchers voted against our motion and I am sure the constituents in western Canada would be very concerned if they realized that their Members of Parliament had voted against those things.
The motion before us today deals not only with agriculture, which is one of our primary industries, but with the forest industry, the energy sector and economic diversification. I am glad the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) is in the House today. I hope he will join in the debate. I know he is feeling extremely uncomfortable these days and we only have to read the report in The Globe and Mail on March 21 to find out why. The Premier of Alberta, the Deputy Prime Minister's home province, has indicated he plans a separation of the Alberta Conservative Party from its federal counterpart if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) does not come up with help soon for the province's ailing economy. The report in The Globe and Mail states:
In the strongest language he has used yet in a continuing fight with Ottawa over the oil-industry aid, Mr. Getty said: "Our provincial party might have to separate in some way from an over-all federal party." In an interview, Mr. Getty emphasized his impatience with the federal Government's refusal to help. "I'm stressing to them time is running out. We're (being hurt) too badly and they don't seem to appreciate it. They must respond in some way. It has to be this year I'd say before summer."
If the Deputy Prime Minister, who lives very close to Edmonton, were to read The Globe and Mail report this morning, March 23, he would see that in several ridings of Edmonton the Tories are running in third place. This is after literally decades of a first-place position. Obviously the Government is not responding to the demands as proposed in the motion before the House today dealing with agriculture, energy, rural diversification in Alberta and the other western provinces, as well as the forestry sector.
Nothing typifies the quandary and concern of Premier Getty of Alberta more than the Syncrude project. Back in the late or mid-1970s, the Syncrude project was foundering even though it was sponsored by several large oil companies. The Liberal
Supply
federal Government at the time came in with a pretty extensive investment of, I believe, some $200 million to get that project going. Last November we received a presentation from the Syncrude people which called upon the federal Government to provide a guarantee agreement of assistance from the federal Government, I believe in the order of $175 million. It was not actual cash. It was not even a loan guarantee. It was simply a guarantee agreement that if the world price of oil fell below $15 a barrel, and it is currently running at $18 or $19 a barrel, the federal Government would provide a loan guarantee at that time. It was unbelievable that the federal Government, which is concerned with energy issues, would not have provided that guarantee agreement. I thought it was really chintzy.
The Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), who is a Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), announced it was his responsibility that the Government had not provided that guarantee agreement. It was simply unbelievable that the Parliamentary Secretary should take the rap for a Government which has the Deputy Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) all from Alberta. It is unbelievable that he should be the goat and say he had not really impressed upon the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the importance of this project. How could those other three members of the federal Cabinet from Alberta sit there and let that project be turned down? The Premier was furious-and he had every right to be so-that the Government would not even provide that guarantee agreement. Of course, the Alberta Government in the end provided the guarantee itself.
That was a signal to people in Alberta, and when our western caucus visited Alberta, during the mid-term break in February, we were told the story that the federal Government had no interest. It was not a case of the cash so much, or that the project would not go ahead, because the Alberta Government went ahead and provided the guarantee, it was the signal that the federal Government was not really committed to the diversification that tar sands programs provide. We are not only talking about the $350 million to expand the capacity by about 20,000 barrels a day, from, I believe it is 125,000 barrels or 130,000 barrels a day to 150,000 barrels a day. The Alberta Government had already put in another $85 million for a doubling of the capacity of Syncrude. That project, provided that world prices do come back, will get underway about 1989 or 1990.
Here we have the federal Government refusing to provide for the interim expansion of the Syncrude projects by some 20,000 barrels a day, which is very important in itself, but also it was going to nix the doubling of capacity, and the provincial Government has had to provide some $85 million to carry out that study. We are talking about a massive expansion which is going to be hobbled because of the federal Government's lack

March 23, 1987
Supply
of commitment to the long-term strategy. I think the upgrading of tar sands plants and heavy oil plants should go ahead. That is very important in the Deputy Prime Minister's riding in terms of jobs. But instead of the cabinet Ministers, the Deputy Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs or even the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who comes from Calgary and has a great stake and interest in the whole energy field, taking the blame for the Government's decision to say no to the oil patch and no to Alberta, the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Athabasca, says it is all his fault, that he did not impress upon the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources its full importance.
In Edmonton today the Tories are running third in the latest opinion polls because they are not prepared to make such a commitment. When our western caucus held hearings in Edmonton, Alberta in mid-February, a second aspect of the Tory energy policy was tremendously rapped by groups such as the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada. I am referring to their decision not to provide assistance under an earned depletion allowance. The Independent Petroleum Association of Canada pointed out before our task force hearings in Edmonton that the Government should have provided in the Budget-and there was nothing to speak of in the Budget; it was really an economic statement-for an earned depletion allowance. In that event we could have seen, for a net cost of some $60 million, a gross allowance of $350 million. It would have been a tax expenditure, but much of it would have been recovered in income taxes and in a reduction in unemployment insurance benefits and welfare costs. We could also have seen an extra 2,000 oil wells being drilled in Alberta and in the western sedimentary basin this summer, as well as the creation of 20,000 jobs. Can we imagine the creation of 20,000 jobs for a net cost of $60 million to the federal Government? It is simply incredible that a Government concerned and interested about unemployment would have turned down such a proposal, not only put to it by IPAC but by CPA and the association representing small drillers.
This week a group representing small drillers was in my office and said that the situation would be absolutely devastating if it continued. As IPAC said in its presentation, it is expected that investment this year will be some $3 billion. Let us compare that with $5.3 billion last year and with $9.5 billion in 1985. The number of oil wells drilled this year in Alberta and in the western sedimentary basin will drop from the 12,564 in 1985 to less than 5,400.
With the simple provision of an earned depletion allowance, the number of wells being drilled would increase to 7,000 this year. Investment would increase to over $4 billion and the cash flow would be $6.6 billion. The loss of reserves would also be held to 48 per cent. Under the present regime, the regime the Government is adopting for the coming year, as indicated in the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), only 34 per cent of those reserves will be replaced.
What did the Government promise in the last election? It promised jobs, jobs, jobs. The then Minister of Energy glibly talked about hundreds of thousands of jobs. It was never possible to pin her down to whether it would be 100,000, 200,000, or 300,000 jobs. However, what have we seen? We have seen thousands of people being put out of work and no commitment in the Budget to provide jobs in the coming year.
A whole new regime has been put before us by the new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, compared with what the Government promised in the last election. Selfsufficiency was an important aspect, but the new Minister said that self-sufficiency was not a realistic goal at this time. He also indicated last fall that job creation was not an important factor in the energy policy and that no questions would be asked if small Canadian companies in trouble were bought out by large U.S. multinational oil companies. The situation is extremely serious in the oil industry, and the motion before the House calls for attention to this situation as well as to agriculture.
I want to talk about the situation in agriculture. At present the circumstances are the most devastating and most uncertain we have seen certainly since the 1930s. About two and a half weeks ago we learned that the price of grain would be about 20 per cent less than it was last year. When that was reported at the Canadian Federation of Agriculture meeting in Hull, Quebec, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) was present and said that he did not know anything about it. It was amazing that the Canadian Wheat Board would have indicated that to members of the advisory committee and to the public, but that the Minister did not know anything about the 20 per cent reduction in initial prices of grains. It was cleared up that afternoon because the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) met with farmers from the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and indicated clearly that the Canadian Wheat Board was calling for a 20 per cent reduction in initial prices.
Let us put it into perspective. This indicates a reduction from $130 per tonne for No. 1 wheat in the current crop year to $110 or perhaps even $105 per tonne. The real prices for No. 2 and No. 3 feed grains would be much lower.
In my motion last week we called upon the Government to provide at least the same returns as those of last year. Taking into account that perhaps the initial price would be 20 per cent less, we called upon the Government to provide returns, along with stabilization or efficiency payments, of at least $ 130 per tonne. What the Minister had to say last week in that debate was very interesting. He quoted his statement of March 5 when he met with grain producers and refused to give a commitment. He quoted as if farmers were saying that they did not want to know what support would be provided. He spent all his time talking about resource neutral payments and so on, but he gave no commitment on what financial assistance would be provided.
Last Friday I had a chance to meet with a number of wheat producers in Manitoba. I told them that the Minister said in
March 23, 1987

the debate last week that the Government would spare no effort. I asked them what would happen if they went to their banks and said that the Minister had given them a commitment that he would spare no effort in providing assistance. One farmer said that if he went to his banker and said that the Minister would spare no effort and gave him 65 cents, his banker would give him a cup of coffee but not a production loan based upon the Minister's comment.
The Minister went into great contortions about how farmers want to base their plantings on market signals and such. In a press release on March 13, the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board said that things did not look very promising this year for price, that he thought we would see most farmers planting, and that it would have to be an individual decision by each farmer. It is blatantly obvious that it must be an individual decision, but we do not know what is the initial price or what will be the financial support.
In the same press report Jack Penner, President of the Keystone Agricultural Producers said, "There is an awful lot of discussion out there whether or not farmers should even seed a crop. We are facing a situation worse than the 1930s if we do not address this. Why should producers go out and seed if they are going to only lose money? Wise has told farmers the decision on the federal aid is not likely before seeding".
We can see that the Government is giving no commitment to the farm sector; no commitment to the energy sector. Obviously it is making no commitment at all to western agriculture or to the western energy sector. It is about time for the Government to come clean and make a clear-cut commitment.

For starters, recognizing that the debate has centred around agriculture to a great extent, I thought the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville might be interested in the following quotation from a representative of the Alberta Wheat Pool which appeared in The Winnipeg Free Press on Thursday, December 18, 1986. Under the heading "Pool Praises PM" we find:
The Alberta Wheat Pool has praised the Government of Prime Minister Brian
Mulroney for its handling of problems in the agriculture industry.
Spokesman Bruno Friesen said yesterday agriculture is facing some of its
toughest times ever and Ottawa has been quick to respond.
"It's really quite an extraordinary hard time in agriculture right now and we
feel that so far the present Government has responded well".
Supply
What better vote of confidence could one have than that, Madam Speaker, having regard to the fact that the pools have traditionally not been noted for exposing any political allegiance to either Party? That is rather significant and we welcome it, as I am sure the Hon. Member does too.

December 18, 1986, page 59.
We recognize, as do all Hon. Members, the very difficult circumstances the west is undergoing with the collapse in commodity prices in agriculture, forestry, mining and energy. Unfortunately, we have heard very little from either the Liberal spokesman or the Hon. Member for Yorkton- Melville concerning solutions. The Member for Yorkton- Melville outlined in a general way what he considered to be a reasonable approach toward economic diversification, the principles upon which I agree.
In brief, we have to remember that we are faced with worldwide oversupply, fierce international competition, export subsidy wars and protectionist measures around the globe, all of which combined have imposed serious pressure on the resource- based industry of western Canada. Commodity prices have fallen. Western Canada has not enjoyed the same robust economic activity experienced in other parts of Canada, particularly in Ontario. Many of these problems first emerged during the previous recession when, combined with the 198182 interest rate spiral, Canadian farmers found themselves in very serious difficulty. That also had a major bearing upon the resource-based industry in western Canada which was in the process of expanding and building. It too got lodged into some very high interest rates.
I am somewhat surprised, and I have a tremendous amount of respect for the Hon. Member from Yorkton-Melville, that his leader, given the importance of this issue, would not have introduced the motion. Is he so preoccupied with gaining political support in Quebec that he finds it a little awkward to support the initiatives and concerns of western Canada?
I noted that the Hon. Member touched on the CF-18 issue. In The Winnipeg Free Press for March 20, 1987, a journalist by the name of Fred Cleverley made the point that the CF-18 issue did not cause much of a discussion at the annual meeting of the New Democratic Party in Montreal. He asked:
Why would Howard Pawley say one thing in Manitoba and another in Montreal? Has he been persuaded that the theft of the CF-18 maintenance contract is less an outrage to Manitoba than he first stated? Would an NDP federal Government act differently from the Liberals and the Conservatives in matters affecting Quebec?
On the contract, the premier's message differs, depending on where he is. New Democrats can count. The figures are Quebec 75, Manitoba 14.
The upshot, Madam Speaker, is that a couple of resolutions were introduced condemning the awarding of the CF-18 contract to Canadair, but neither saw the light of day. While New Democrats are critical of the CF-18 contract, they do not clearly state a position. Certainly that is part of the challenge of being a national Party. What we are seeing now, I suppose,

March 23, 1987
is a certain maturing of the New Democratic Party. It is now looking for support in the Province of Quebec.
The Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) on a number of occasions has tried to raise the profile of agriculture and its difficulties. He has been proposing in Question Period that we should have guaranteed grain prices equal to this year's prices. We are not satisfied with the prices being paid to Canadian farmers today. Certainly we must do better. We have cushioned the difficult problem farmers face through deficiency payments, the reduction of input costs and by the removal of fuel taxes. Interest rates have come down.
As well, we have been tackling this issue on the international front. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister of State for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) have been working very closely with farmers both here in Canada and in the international community. Progress is being made, Madam Speaker. But when the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party suggests that the federal Government should force the Canadian Wheat Board to establish artificially high prices, on reflection, I think Hon. Members across the way should consider what they are proposing. They are really proposing a policy of obstruction and interference in the affairs of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board Act is pretty specific. It says this in terms of establishing initial prices:
The Board shall-
Not may.
-with the approval of the Governor-in-Council, determine and fix the
amounts to which producers are entitled per tonne according to grade and the
certificates issued pursuant to this Part-
It does not say that the Governor-in-Council shall with the approval of the Board. It says "The Board shall with the approval of the Governor-in-Council". That is a very important difference. I am surprised that the New Democratic Party would engage in this vicious attack upon the principles and the orderly marketing concept of the Canadian Wheat Board.

subsubtopic: POSTAL RATES INCREASE-CONSEQUENCES FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM-SIZED BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Last week, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government approved a first class letter 2-cent postage increase.
I quote the Canada Post press release:
Most additional revenues will come from higher rates on market competing
commercial services. Only 30 per cent of Canada Post revenues originate from
basic rate letters, the remaining 70 per cent being accounted for by its
commercial sector clients.
Mr. Speaker, these 150,000 small and medium-sized businesses operate in Canada and are Canada Post service main users. This is a vital and essential postal service, and such businesses are again hard hit by the Canadian Government.
Ever since the Progressive Conservatives came into office, Mr. Speaker, they have never advocated a small business policy nor any program to boost the expansion of this very important sector which creates most new jobs in this country. Once again faced with higher postal rates, small business will end up paying for this $122 million increase.

subtopic: GRAIN OVER-PRODUCTION-CALL FOR CONVERSION TO ETHANOL
GRAIN OVER-PRODUCTION-CALL FOR CONVERSION TO ETHANOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one disputes that a global over-production brought about by government subsidy programs has resulted in the low grain prices which are devastating Canadian grain and oil-seed producers. Even though the Canadian Government has shown a commitment to see farmers through this crisis, every effort must be made to provide a long-term solution to global over-production of grain.
One answer is becoming more and more obvious. We could put surplus grain directly into our gasoline tanks in the form of ethanol alcohol blended with gasoline. As well as consuming excess grain, it would improve the environment because clean burning alcohol can successfully replace lead as an octane enhancer.
U.S.-Vice President George Bush has initiated a thrust of increasing the use of ethanol in U.S. gas blends by 2.5 billion gallons. This would consume an additional one billion bushels of surplus corn over what is already in ethanol production. If Canada followed that lead and in turn helped convince other grain producing nations to do the same, we would provide the solution to the woes of the Canadian grain farmer at the least cost to the taxpayer.
March 23, 1987

Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has been playing with the future of western Canadian sugar beet producers by delaying yet again a decision on a national sugar policy. In 1985, in return for $2.9 million from Manitoba to the province's producers, the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board who has been charged with developing sugar policy said in a telegram that "the federal Government-will not require any further financial participation beyond the 1985 crop". Then, without consultation, he and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) unilaterally announced a tripartite stabilization plan requiring the provinces to pay one-third of the premiums and to be liable for one-half of the deficit.
Neither the producers nor the provinces have asked for such a plan. What they wanted was a clear national sugar and sweetener policy that would provide long-term viability. What they have is continued delay and lack of direction.

subtopic: INVESTMENT TAX CREDIT AUDIT-VALUATION OF TRADED-IN AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT
INVESTMENT TAX CREDIT AUDIT-VALUATION OF TRADED-IN AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Revenue Canada is going as far back as 1983 to review the tax returns of hundreds of Canadian farmers who, in good faith, utilized the business investment tax credit on purchases of new farm machinery. When making a deal most farmers are interested only in the cash difference between the new item and the trade-in. They do not care how the paperwork is done. It is the cash difference that matters.
In cases where the dealer has exceeded the list or manufacturer's suggested retail price, there may be abuse and few would argue with that. However, the normal trade plus cash deal where the list price is not exceeded ought not to be the topic of a departmental witch-hunt. Yet it appears that Revenue Canada is questioning the valuation of equipment traded in ordinary, every-day, bona fide, arm's-length transactions, and substituting instead its own opinions. I suggest that in doing so Revenue Canada is treading on very thin ice. I urge the Minister to instruct his officials to cease and desist from this arbitrary and dangerous departure from practices in the market-place and from previous policy.

subtopic: ACID RAIN-NEED FOR UNITED STATES PROGRAM
ACID RAIN-NEED FOR UNITED STATES PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would praise President Reagan for promising this year to do something next year to keep a promise he made last year on acid rain. Now is the time for the Prime Minister to speak frankly and to say that what Canadians want from the United States Government is a program designed to cut acid rain by a certain date, by a certain percentage, and in a manner that is meaningful to Canada.
Washington showed political will when it got Mexico to cut acid rain damaging the U.S. That political will must be generated again with respect to Canada which is downwind from U.S. emissions. The summit is less than two weeks away. We urge the Prime Minister to get off his knees and stand up for Canada.
