subtopic: USE OF FORMER CANADIAN MILITARY AIRCRAFT BY TURKISH AIR FORCE
USE OF FORMER CANADIAN MILITARY AIRCRAFT BY TURKISH AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year the Government assured me that giving CF-104 fighter aircraft to Turkey would not affect the delicate political situation in the eastern Mediterranean. However, on March 5 Canadian Press reported that 100 Kurdish rebels were killed by Turkish F-104s on bombing raids into neighbouring Iraq. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) could not answer my questions about this incident in committee that day. He later sent a letter which said, "It is impossible to confirm whether or not former Canadian aircraft were used by the Turkish Air Force". The Turkish Government would say only that the F-104s were not used in a way which would violate the transfer agreement. That is not good enough.
Those fighter planes would not be in Turkey if it was not for the help of the Conservative Government. Canada has a responsibility to see that those planes are not used for air strikes into neighbouring states. I call on the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to investigate the incident and report to this House. Canadians must be assured that we are not contributing to violence and instability in the Middle East.

Mr. Speaker, something is drastically wrong with our National Parole Board and the entire parole system. Recent Parole Board decisions have cast serious doubts on its ability to protect Canadians. In the past month two very dangerous individuals were released. It was only after a public outcry that their paroles were revoked.
The latest Parole Board mistake was the release of an individual who was sentenced to nine years for the attempted murder of a Toronto police officer. During sentencing the judge called the act "deliberate, clearly motivated, callous and cold-blooded". Yet the Parole Board released him after he had served only three and a half years. Have these people lost all sense of justice? The Parole Board is in place to protect innocent Canadians, not side with criminals. Individuals who commit severe acts must pay, otherwise our entire justice system will become a joke.
I call on the Government to initiate a thorough review of the criteria and procedures used by the NPB in order that justice be served.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
On several occasions, Mr. Speaker, I told the House that as a result of its inaction the Conservative Government sows discontent in all levels of society. The latest examples have to do with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the official languages, the linguistic training programs, and the various Public Service dismantling projects.
As reported by the media, inaptitude at its worst can be seen in the fact that discontent now reaches into Government ranks. The Conservative caucus is divided. This morning we learned that certain members had made unpleasant remarks. Ministers publicly say that members are minor chronic complainers. Newspaper reports indicate that the series of ministerial resignations might be followed by more resignations by members. Next in line to go after the Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin) might be the Member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead (Mr. Gerin), the Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon), or the Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin). They too know as we do that this Government is unable to provide leadership, and they have lost faith in this Government. They want to exercise their democratic rights as members and representatives of the people, but Ministers tell them to shut up, that they are nothing but minor chronic complainers. It takes a minor boss to know a minor chronic complainer!

Mr. Speaker, this past weekend Metro Toronto's more than 100,000 Canadians of Greek origin celebrated the 166th anniversary of Greek independence with a magnificent banquet and a huge parade along Danforth Avenue. At the banquet on Saturday night Professor Steve Triantis of the University of Toronto delivered a message for all politicians to heed. He said:
Governments in Canada have underestimated and treated with affront the intelligence and power of the so-called ethnic communities, two-fifths of the population of this country. We shall demand full and equal participation in the political, social, cultural and economic life of this country. We have indications that the federal Government has realized the problem and is taking steps to correct it. We shall be looking for action in particular with regards to appointments to boards and agencies.
The leaders of all political parties should be advised that no ethnic group in Canada holds a monopoly of excellence in brains and education and that political parties that wish to find any excuse for being a charmed circle of the select, rubbing shoulders with each other and taking care of each other, will remain parties of the few.
March 23, 1987

Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa has decided not to attend the meetings of First Ministers and Native People to establish aboriginal rights.
The former Premier of Quebec, Mr. Levesque, attended those meetings, despite the fact that the Constitution did not recognize the special character and needs of Quebec.
Mr. Levesque recognized his responsibility for 35,000 Indians, 6,000 Inuit and a large number of Metis in his province.
The native peoples want what the people of Quebec want: to be masters of their own fate. Mr. Bourassa should recognize their needs and his responsibility.

subtopic: CREATION OF SULPHURIC ACID AT ROUYN-NORANDA
CREATION OF SULPHURIC ACID AT ROUYN-NORANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Ottawa-Quebec agreement on acid rain signed in Montreal last Friday is of course a major event for this country, but even more so for Rouyn-Noranda and the Abitibi-Temiscamingue area.
On March 20, this Government signed an agreement with the Government of Quebec and Noranda Mines to help build a sulphuric acid plant in Rouyn-Noranda at an estimated cost of $125 million, a plant that will help Noranda Mines to reduce its S02 emissions by 50 per cent.
The economic impact will also be quite considerable. Within the next three years 265 jobs will be created, and 55 permanent jobs by 1990.
Mr. Speaker, this is a great victory for the people of my area, because it is the culmination of plans that have been in the works for quite some time. I am proud of the way the Government has discharged its responsibilities in a project that is aimed at improving the quality of life of my fellow citizens.

subtopic: POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY IN ALBERTA
POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY IN ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party is in a panic. The situation is so
bad that in the Province of Alberta the P.C. Leader thinks one of the ways of getting out of their problem is separating from the federal Party. Further exacerbating the anxiety of the Conservatives is the new poll which shows that the people of Edmonton are split across all three party lines. That means that for the first time in a very long time the Liberal Party has a chance of winning seats in Edmonton. The reason for that is that we have been working very closely with the Liberal caucus in Alberta, the finest of the three caucuses there.
With regard to a situation like C-14, who has been speaking for the people of Alberta? Has the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) spoken out and said that he will not allow services to be taken out of the health care plan in Alberta? No, he has sat back and taken a hands-off position as universal accessibility to medicare for the people of Alberta continues to be threatened.
We in the Liberal Opposition here will be fighting. We will be working closely with our colleagues in the provincial Legislature. We will not only roll back Bill C-14, we will ensure that such an assault on medicare occurs in no other province in the country.

subtopic: ACID RAIN-NEW NORANDA PLANT TO REDUCE SULPHUR DIOXIDE EMISSIONS
ACID RAIN-NEW NORANDA PLANT TO REDUCE SULPHUR DIOXIDE EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Government realizes the serious threat of acid rain but it is also committed to assisting the industry in its move to correct this international problem. An example of this commitment was seen Friday with the announcement of a $125 million agreement with Noranda at the Rouyn-Noranda copper smelter. The announced new plant is designed to remove 96 per cent of sulphur dioxide contained in the production gases from the smelter's reactor.
The $41.6 million loan by the federal Government will go a long way to help the company meet the goal of 50 per cent reduction in sulphur dioxide emissions by 1990. Just as important though, this agreement provides stability to the future of the industry and the assurance of 6,000 jobs within this region.
This latest announcement is very good news for the people of northern Ontario and Quebec. It is a fine example of how the Government is meeting the challenge of reducing acid rain emissions while strengthening the industry.

March 23, 1987
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: THE ARCTIC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We know that the Prime Minister and the Government have caved in on fish, energy, foreign investment, drug prices and softwood lumber. Last week they backtracked on acid rain. Is this week's cave-in the Canadian Arctic?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: THE ARCTIC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the cave-in in the Canadian Arctic occurred years before, under a Liberal Government. This Progressive Conservative Government has acted to assert Canada's control and sovereignty over the Arctic.
There were false news reports emanating from a story by Mr. Peter Newman. Those reports were corrected by some conscientious journalists and correct reports appeared in The Ottawa Citizen and The Toronto Star last night. The CBC ran false reports again this morning. I am not sure why the CBC would choose to run those false reports.

subtopic: UNITED STATES RECOGNITION OF CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: UNITED STATES RECOGNITION OF CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs confirm that the Canadian Government is not negotiating our sovereignty over the Canadian Arctic? Will he confirm that the price for having the Americans recognize our waters as Canadian waters in our Arctic, not international waters, the price for American recognition of that sovereignty is not an agreement from the Americans not to respect it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: UNITED STATES RECOGNITION OF CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition became a little twisted in the expression of his second question. Perhaps he was trying to get unanimity in his whole Party by being confusing as to what he was saying. Here are the facts.
In September, 1985, when we announced the dramatic action to assert Canada's sovereignty over our north, I also indicated that we would be entering into discussions with the United States to see if there was some way we could have an arrangement that would serve their legitimate security interests and respect our sovereignty. Those discussions have been going on since that time and are continuing. I want to make the point that if there is a failure in those discussions, or if we are not satisfied that Canadian sovereignty will be respected, we are prepared to defend our claims to our north before the International Court of Justice, as the former Liberal Government was afraid to do.

subtopic: UNITED STATES RECOGNITION OF CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister invariably seeks to rewrite Canada's history, but I suggest that Canadians will not be fooled.

I am already involved in serious consultations with the Government leaders of the two great North Territories with respect to the controversy which Americans call the 1002 question.

Mr. Speaker, you will recall at the time of the so-called Arctic icebreaker contract award that the Secretary of State for External Affairs said it was an assertion of Canadian sovereignty over the Northwest Passage. Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

Did you discuss it with them?
March 23, 1987

Hamilton East. I told the Americans what we were doing. I did not ask their permission but I told them we were building an ice-breaker to establish our sovereignty in our north.

There is no connection between the decision to build a Canadian ice-breaker to protect our sovereignty and Mr. Reagan's visit. Our sovereignty is not negotiable. They were afraid to put the Canadian position and Canadian sovereignty before the International Court of Justice. As far as we are concerned, the age of fear has come to an end.

Mr. Speaker, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs quite explicitly assure the House that in the negotiations he is having with the United States there are not any discussions or negotiations on the question of Canadian sovereignty, that that is accepted and that the United States has not in fact and will not in fact be given full and free access to Canadian Arctic waters?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

Mr. Speaker, as I have just said in the House, we have declared our sovereignty over the north, as former Governments declined to do. As I indicated in my statement in the House in September of 1985, we are discussing with the United States the possibility of some arrangement that would

respect our sovereignty and meet its legitimate security interests. As I said in September of 1985 and as I said again a moment ago in response to the question of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, if we do not secure an agreement respecting our sovereignty, that is satisfactory to Canada, then those discussions will stop and we will be prepared to defend our sovereignty before the International Court of Justice, as the previous Liberal Government was afraid to do.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE-UNITED STATES-JAPAN AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. An agreement has been signed, but not ratified, between the United States and Japan concerning the transport of nuclear fuel using Canadian airspace. There are grave concerns about whether a container safe enough to transport these large amounts of plutonium which are being contemplated can ever be built.
In light of those concerns, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs ensure that both those countries know before they ratify that agreement that Canadians and the Government of Canada do not want our airspace to be used for the transport of nuclear fuel?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE-UNITED STATES-JAPAN AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman might have noticed from the newspaper story he obviously read this morning that it is a draft agreement not ratified by either country. In any event, transportation of radioactive material by air is subject to an international convention as well as to Canadian legislation. It is subject to the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act and regulations thereunder to the Atomic Energy Control Act and regulations thereunder and to Annex 18 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation, so we would have several options if such overflights were proposed. First, we can request that pre-notification be given and that approval be received prior to an overflight, or we can deny an overflight by filing a state difference with ICAO. In either case, of course, we would insist on stringent requirements for packaging and adequate inspection and that everything be observed which is necessary for the transportation of radioactive materials. The hon. gentleman can rest assured that these are all matters which will be insisted upon.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE-UNITED STATES-JAPAN AGREEMENT
speechtext: I am sure Canadians will insist that their airspace not be used to transport nuclear fuel.

REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION THROUGH ICAO

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION THROUGH ICAO

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF SULPHURIC ACID PLANT AT ROUYN-NORANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment.
Following the historic agreement on acid rain signed with Quebec last Friday in Montreal, I would like to ask the Minister what impact building a sulphuric acid plant in Rouyn-Noranda will have on the objectives being pursued by Quebec and Canada in terms of reducing air pollution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: IMPACT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF SULPHURIC ACID PLANT AT ROUYN-NORANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the plant mentioned by the Hon. Member for Temiscamingue is of great importance for the environment. In fact, the federal Government is contributing one third of the cost of financing the project, in other words, nearly $42 million. The plant will make it possible for Noranda Mines to reduce its sulphuric acid emissions by 50 per cent by 1990.
This proves the Government of Canada is prepared to put up funds toward meeting its commitment to reduce acid rain.
The Hon. Member is to be commended for his co-operation. I appreciate this very much.

subsubtopic: CANADA-FRANCE DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries said in a November 24, 1986, press release: "We are under no legal obligation to give the French any fish in Canadian waters". Despite no legal obligation, talks will start tomorrow morning, Tuesday morning, with the French Government, in Ottawa, to figure out how much fish to give away to the French for the four-year period from 1988 to 1991. Since the Prime Minister said that no fish would be given to the French unless Newfoundland agrees and Newfoundland has said "no", and since the Minister of Transport has said "not one fish, not one tail, not one head, not one fillet", what is northern cod doing on the agenda of the talks
Oral Questions
with the French Government which start Tuesday morning in Ottawa? We are being gutted again by the Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: CANADA-FRANCE DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has already been gutted head on according to his question. He partially quoted the Minister of Fisheries. On November 26 the Minister of Fisheries said:
We have told the French that under the 1972 treaty we have no obligation to provide them with any fish-
And I go on to complete the quotation:
-to replace what they have been catching in the Gulf and, specifically, no obligation to provide them with any northern cod, over and above allocations made under the Fisheries Agreement with the EEC, which expires at the end of 1987.
Our only obligations to the French to give them fish at all were caused by the treaty of 1972, entered into by the Liberal Government of the day, and by the treaty of 1982 entered into with the EEC. I hope the hon. gentleman will apologize when he next gets to his feet.
In addition, at these discussions tomorrow, the hon. gentleman will be happy to know that the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception and the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's will be present. There will be a strong Newfoundland delegation. I will have a representative there, and I can assure him that we will be well represented in those discussions.

Mr. Speaker, the Department of External Affairs said today that a quota will be negotiated. The Canadian Embassy in Paris said that a quota will be negotiated. The federal Department of Fisheries said that a quota will be negotiated. Does the Minister really expect Canadian fishermen to believe a Minister who closes Canadian ports after the French have gone home? Can he guarantee us now that the first thing he will do tomorrow morning, during these negotiations, is to remove northern cod from that menu? Let them eat cake.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter which has been on the menu with the French since 1972 when the Liberal Government, which was supported by the hon. gentleman, put it on the menu in a treaty that has no termination date. It is on the menu every year from now on, indefinitely. It is a Liberal menu put there by the Liberals. That is why it is on the menu.
The hon. gentleman asked about closing the ports. Our Liberal predecessors never closed the ports to French fishing vessels, nor did they ever close Burgeo Bank to French fishing. The next time the hon. gentleman rises to his feet, will he explain to Canadians why in 1982 they signed away 47,500 tonnes of prime northern cod to France and other nations in the European Economic Community? Let us hear no more from the hon. gentleman.

Oral Questions HUNTING OF MATURE SEALS

Mr. Speaker, last week two East Coast Canadian companies announced that they would be sending ships to the front off the East Coast of Newfoundland and Labrador to hunt mature seals. On Saturday the Department of Fisheries and Oceans notified these companies to suspend their operations until further notice. Will the Acting Minister of Fisheries assure these companies and the House today that the Government of Canada will not impede their legitimate operations to harvest a renewable resource? Will he also assure us that we will not see those sealers harassed by so-called anti-seal protesters?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to answer a question from a mariner who knows what he is talking about, not a baker who does not know what he is talking about.
Let him bake cake.

I hope he gets a rise out of that one.
The Fisheries Minister is announcing today that strict controls are being placed on all companies with large vessels participating in the seal harvest this year. They will be permitted to participate. The seal hunt is not illegal in Canada. The Minister is asking for and obtaining a written undertaking that they will take no white coats. In other words, they will not take any baby seals or seals of that age. The Minister is announcing that this is entirely consistent with the recommendations of the Malouf Royal Commission on seals and the sealing industry which found sealing to be a humane and economically significant industry that posed no threat to the seal population. Two inspectors will be placed in each vessel to ensure that the seal hunt is humane and that all regulations are observed. I hope that satisfies the Hon. Member's query.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO U.S. SECRETARY OF ENERGY
speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO U.S. SECRETARY OF ENERGY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the short answer is that I am not familiar with the particular quotation from Secretary of Energy John Herrington to which the Hon. Member has referred. March 23, 1987

Tell us.

subsubtopic: PROSPECTIVE LEBANESE IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:

Because of an indifferent and uncaring Minister, these individuals had to be stranded for four days at airports in both Madrid and Athens and are now reportedly in a jail cell in Cyprus.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: PROSPECTIVE LEBANESE IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:

speechtext: It is my unhappy responsibility to draw to the attention of all Hon. Members the death of the Hon. Walter Gordon, a distinguished former Member of this House and member of the Privy Council. It would be appropriate to hear comments and I call upon the Right Hon. speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I walked into the House at 2.15, I learned of the death of Walter Gordon on Saturday. He was well known to several Members of this House of Commons having sat as the Hon. Member for Davenport from 1962 to 1968, and having served as Minister of Finance from 1962 to 1965 in the Government of the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson.
Prior to his election to the House of Commons he had a very distinguished career. He was one of our country's leading chartered accountants and one of its first management
The Late Walter Gordon
consultants, first with the firm of Clarkson Gordon, and then Woods Gordon. He was perhaps best noted prior to his election to this House as Chairman of the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects, 1955. That was an immense piece of work which influenced economic thinking in this country for the following generation.
Since his retirement from public life he has had a very remarkable career. He was Chancellor of York University, one of the founders of the Committee for an Independent Canada, President of Canadian Corporate Management, a hugely successful Canadian-owned company. Among his major interests he was a Director of The Toronto Star. He was an author. Most of us have read some or all of his books such as, Troubled Canada, A Choice for Canada, Storm Signals, A Political Memoir, What is Happening to Canada.
Mr. Gordon was among those people who considered public service to be the highest calling in a free country. I think I can say that he has been the most influential of our Canadian economic nationalists. He was a pioneer in seeking an economically independent Canada. I can tell you that he was deeply concerned by the current free trade negotiations. An open letter he wrote to me on the pages of The Toronto Star last October had this paragraph:
I have long been convinced that a large majority of Canadians wants our country to remain free and independent, or as free and independent as is practicable in this interdependent world. Certainly we do not wish ever to become part of the United States or to agree to policies that could lead in that direction such as the proposed free trade deal.
He cared passionately as well for the dispossessed and disadvantaged of this country and, although born to relatively easy circumstances, devoted a good deal of his professional and political life to re-establishing a better equality in our country. We knew him as a man of tremendous ability, of sensitive manners, warm personality and infectious sense of humour. Perhaps the words which might characterize him superbly would be "a civilized man".
Liberals remember him as one of the seminal influences of the renewal of this Party from 1958 to 1968. He was among our best loved figures. Denis Smith qualified him in his biography of Mr. Gordon as "that gentle patriot". He loved this Canada he served so well and with such altruistic distinction.
In personal terms, Mr. Speaker, I was proud to have known him well, to have counted him as a friend and a counsellor. On my own behalf, on behalf of the Party I lead, and on behalf of a legion of friends across Party boundaries, I offer to his widow Liz and their three children our heartfelt condolences and our total admiration.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one did not have to agree with all of the works and attitudes of Walter Gordon to share a profound

The Late Walter Gordon
respect for his contribution to his country, his Party, and this Parliament. He was a man of outstanding accomplishment in both public and private life. On behalf of the Government, my Party, and my Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) I want to associate myself with the words uttered by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).
We all felt a great sadness when we learned of the death of Walter Gordon. He combined outstanding careers in both the public and private sectors. As the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition said, he was one of Canada's leading chartered accountants and then became one of our leading management consultants.
However, it was really in the public sector, in the service of the country, that Walter Gordon most distinguished himself; first as a Royal commissioner of a vast, often controversial, but highly imaginative and wholly Canadian commission into the economic future of our country; then as a cabinet Minister; and then not simply as an architect of the rebirth of the Liberal Party in the early days of the 1960s but, more than that, as the force around whom the reformers who wanted to bring new life and new perspective to that Party gathered, the active force which gave it direction. He was, of course, a committed and persuasive Canadian nationalist.
I think of Walter Gordon as a reformer, a man who was prepared to challenge old ideas and also prepared to work to change them. I think of him as a man of honour who was prepared to follow the highest dictates of Canadian parliamentary life, even when they were difficult for him to follow. Throughout his life he was a thorough gentleman, a model for others in public life, a model for Canadians through time. On the Prime Minister's behalf and on behalf of all those in my Party, I want to express our condolences to his widow and family and our respect for the example he has given this country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on this very sad day in this tribute to the Hon. Walter Gordon. Everything that has been said about him is so true. If I may, for just a moment I would like to put a personal perspective on what has been said.
The Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the way in which Walter Gordon gave direction and courage to the reforming element in the Liberal Party. I was in the Party at that time and he was certainly the beacon for me as well as for many others who joined the Party then. It began for me at the Kingston Conference and continued right through our common period in the House of Commons.
For example, when I was a back-bencher in the fifth row on the far side I sat almost directly behind Walter Gordon. Walter would bring together an interested group of young Turks, as we were sometimes called, who were interested in
genuine social and economic reform in Canada. He would have meetings with us at regular intervals and include us in discussions on any Bills he was going to bring into Parliament. I can remember Bills on the establishment of the Economic Council of Canada and many other measures while he was Minister of Finance. He made us feel very much a part of the system. I am speaking of many years ago; 1963, 1964, and 1965.
It was during this period also that he encouraged us to really think, some of us for the very first time, about what Canada really meant, about our slide into continentalism, about our need for an independent economic strategy, our need for Canadian ownership of resources and secondary manufacturing, and our need for an independent Canadian foreign policy. There were touches of this, of course, in the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects in the late 1950s and again at the Kingston Conference, but they came to full bloom during his period as Minister of Finance and after that in the House of Commons in the 1960s.
Indeed he was "a gentle patriot" as Professor Denis Smith called him in his biography. 1 guess that is one reason why even those who disagreed with him loved him. He was really universally loved in this country; perhaps not always as loved south of the border from time to time, but always respected. His leadership in forming and developing the Committee for an Independent Canada, of which I and many other Members here today were early or founding members, was incredibly strong. He did alert the Canadian public to the need for a genuine independent Canadian economic strategy and as complete as possible Canadian ownership of the economy.
He was as concerned also with the disadvantaged. His appeals for social progress were as strong as his appeals for economic independence and an independent foreign policy. He had an enormous impact on so many of us. It was really a shock, since I was talking to him not long ago, to learn that he died on Saturday. It is a great loss to Canada and, indeed, to all members of all Parties, not only in Canada but in many other parts of the world.
On behalf of all New Democrats, who, I may say, in the 1960s thought very highly of Walter Gordon too and tried to urge him to come over, I would like to say how sad we are at his dying and how very much we want to send our compassionate best wishes to his widow Liz and the family.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) said, Walter Gordon was the Member of Parliament until 1968 for Davenport. He came to Ottawa in 1962 and was instrumental with former Prime Minister Pearson in the return of the Liberal Party to Government in the early 1960s. Walter Gordon fought many battles. He was motivated by a strong sense of justice in providing Canadians a worth-while social security system. He was motivated by a strong dedication to the protection of the less strong in society. He was a strong

player in the movement for strengthening Canadian ownership of our economy. He was an instigator of a broad policy which eventually resulted in the formation of the Canada Development Corporation, the Foreign Investment Review Agency, and was an enthusiastic supporter of the National Energy Program.
Walter Gordon was a man of great integrity, honesty, and dedication to the public interest. He was reserved and even shy, but motivated by a strong passion for Canada which we, as new Canadians in Toronto, readily understood. Walter Gordon leaves a vacuum in the movement for maintaining Canadian independence. He leaves a vacuum in the movement for disarmament and peace. He leaves a vacuum in the movement by Canadians who are dedicated to the protection and strengthening of Canadian sovereignty.

Mr. Speaker, in resuming debate on this very important motion that has been presented by the Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), let me say that one of the characteristics of the New Democratic Party that occasionally troubles me is their penchant for doom and gloom and negativism. The House will recall that when we announced the $1 billion grain assistance program it was greeted with

derision, if not outright condemnation by the New Democratic Party. Immediately they set out to try to sow the seeds of mistrust and skepticism by suggesting to Canadians and farmers in particular that it would not happen and would only consist of money coming from other agricultural programs, that it would be taken out of the stabilization program, that it would be a loan, or it would be provincial moneys. They wanted to know whether it was new money and where we would find it.
If one looks at Hansard beginning with October 3, 1986, one can see that it is filled with these vicious attacks on the Government, particularly on the Prime Minister, for coming to the aid of western Canadian farmers. That sort of misleading conduct is shameful, especially at a time when we are all trying to do our best to deal with these issues.
The fact is that the money is being received in a manner that has been recommended by the producers. Never before in the history of the country have we seen the kind of cooperation and support from the agricultural community about how to deal with this very important issue. That dialogue is continuing in spite of what my good colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), refers to as the nattering nabobs of negativism. The work is going on with the agricultural community. After the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) met with 55 farm representatives representing 35 farm organizations, he issued a press release on March 5 indicating that progress is being made. We must put these things into perspective.
All of us know that the problems facing western Canada are not simple or easy to resolve. It will require a coherent longterm approach involving government, business, labour, and all sectors of the economy. That will have to be balanced with firm and aggressive action on the international front.
Our Party began that process during the recession in 1983, recognizing even then the challenges and obstacles facing the west. Our efforts culminated in the Prince Albert Declaration which contained a broad range of policies which would promote economic development in the key sectors of the western region. Some 52 specific commitments were made at that time. Of 16 commitments made in agriculture, 14 have been fulfilled. There were 12 commitments made in energy and 10 of them were fulfilled. There were nine commitments in forestry, seven of which have been fulfilled. There were six commitments in mining and four have been fulfilled. Of nine commitments in grain transportation, eight have been fulfilled. That represents 43 out of 52 commitments that have been fulfilled.
Since assuming office many other initiatives have been taken to meet urgent questions, such as the drought payments, the question of action on imports of beef from the EEC and others, and the removal of the unfair energy taxes in the energy sector. The removal of the farm fuel tax works out to some 33.75 cents per gallon. I was interested to note that the

March 23, 1987

Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville advocated an increase in farm fuel prices because he was talking about a floor price for oil which would have the effect of driving up prices.
Our action on interest rates is another major element. In 1982-83, the interest rates were hovering at 22 per cent to 24 per cent. Today, the Bank of Canada rate is down to 7.14 per cent, the lowest in 14 years. We have provided the capital gains exemption for farmers, introduced interest rate reduction programs and debt review boards. We amended the Western Grain Transportation Act and amended the Grain Stabilization Act. We dismantled the National Energy Program and dismantled FIRA. We removed the confiscatory back-in provision.
There have been many initiatives, none of which singularly and perhaps collectively are a magic panacea, but they do represent a substantial improvement. The Prince Albert Declaration demonstrated our government's commitment to address the challenges facing western Canada. We addressed the issues on the basis of building upon our strengths, and the success in fulfilling those commitments provides us with building blocks on which to take further steps.
Since 1984, many other initiatives have been taken in concert with the Prince Alberta Declaration. As the United States-European Economic Community grain subsidy war escalated, we provided $1 billion worth of relief. We accelerated the removal of the PGRT. We worked out a deal with the U.S. on softwood and lumber. That deal was supported by all western premiers. We launched the historic trade initiative, of crucial significance to western Canada.
We have initiated the new National Transportation Act. Again, the Hon. Member said three or four times that there is a need to address the transportation problems and the discriminatory features of our current transportation system. Once and for all, with the passage of the new National Transportation Act, freight rate discrimination in western Canada will be a thing of the past. Why are the New Democrats against it? The two very fundamental matters we are addressing in western Canada, the trade issue and the transportation issue, are being fought right to the wall by the NDP and they should be ashamed of themselves.
We have embarked upon ways and means to utilize western coal in Ontario to a greater extent. Contracts have been awarded to Microtel Systems in British Columbia for high technology equipment for the North Warning Systems. The CF-5 contract was awarded to Winnipeg, with spin-off benefits to Edmonton. The CF-18 contract had corresponding spin-off benefits to Edmonton. The minting of the new dollar coin was awarded to Sherritt-Gordon in Fort Saskatchewan. These are all important elements in diversifying western Canada's economy.
We have signed federal-provincial agreements in all four provinces covering urban development, irrigation, tourism,
agricultural processing, industrial development, science and technology, forestry and small business. Since the new year we have announced that Versatile Pacific will build a new Polar 8 ice-breaker at a cost of something in the order of $350 million, a very major initiative. We have announced $100 million in canola oil purchases for Food Aid. We have facilitated and supported the sale of Versatile Farm Equipment which will reestablish itself on a permanent basis in Winnipeg. It will be good for western Canada and good for the western Canadian farmer.
We have made a number of announcements with respect to forestry. My colleague, the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew), announced a $13 million program with his B.C. counterpart for the establishment of a Canada-British Columbia forest resource development agreement, as well as a science and technology exchange program. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) announced the establishment of a Pacific Rim national park on Vancouver Island.
These are all very important initiatives. Time does not permit me to go on in more detail. Suffice it to say that we will continue to identify and work with the provinces and industry in dealing with these very important issues.
I wish to deal quickly with the issue of energy because it has been raised. I was rather interested in the proposal emanating from the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) which, as I see it, would drive up the price of fuel, in particular farm fuel. I can advise the House that discussions have been taking place in an intensified way with the Government of the Province of Alberta, and other provincial Governments, as well as with industry, in an attempt to deal with the energy sector and the very difficult period it is going through. We have discussed the need to attract investment capital and the need to stimulate drilling, exploration and development. I can advise the House that these talks are going very well. I am sure that within the not too distant future there will be a major announcement with respect to addressing the needs of the energy sector in western Canada.
With respect to western diversification, over the past two and a half years we have responded to the situation, albeit in very tight financial circumstances. I note that the Hon. Member talked about the difficulties that provinces were having with respect to deficits. Because the Hon. Member played a part in creating the burden of debt that was inflicted upon the Canadian people during the four years he and his Party supported the Government of the day formed by the Liberal Party, he should know that the net public debt increased from $85 billion to $200 billion in those four years. That is scandalous. Now the Hon. Member and his Party sympathize with the provinces, but they are indeed the architects of huge deficits.
It is interesting to note as well that the NDP Budget in Manitoba hits the lower income people the hardest.

speechtext:
We recognize that more needs to be done to renew and re-energize the economy of western Canada. We intend to build on our previous efforts in a comprehensive and orderly fashion.
Last September's Speech from the Throne committed the federal Government to placing special emphasis on diversifying the economic base of western Canada, a pledge that has since been reaffirmed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Western Canada has a wealth of resources: physical, capital and human. The federal Government is committed to playing a leadership role in harnessing those resources and overcoming the obstacles and the challenges which confront us.
As I have indicated in this Chamber before, the Government will be coming forward shortly with a western economic initiative as a fundamental component of its regional development strategy. This initiative will provide a framework for growth across western Canada. It is being developed consistent with the Government's broad economic agenda as outlined in November, 1984, under the agenda for economic renewal. Our objective will be to continue to seek new opportunities for traditional resource sectors, whether it be through increased value-added and secondary processing in livestock, forestry and mining or crop diversification, aquaculture, market penetration or productivity enhancement. If the resource sectors are to continue to play an important role in our economy we must improve our access to world markets. In that connection it is important to pare down the barriers to trade. At the same time our objective will be to identify those opportunities in newly emerging high technology sectors, and the key secondary and service sectors such as petrochemicals, aerospace, transportation, tourism and financial services.
We believe that western Canada has the potential to become a world leader in technology in the areas of medical research, biotechnology, micro-electronics and others. We must recognize these opportunities and work with the provincial Governments, with industry and our universities to achieve that potential. Specific initiatives contained in the western development package will be announced in due course. It will reflect the following guiding principles. The private sector will be seen as the engine of economic growth. Trade enhancement and the removal of obstacles to growth are indeed an important component of this initiative. We must create a positive climate of investment to attract new investment capital into western Canada. Our emphasis will also be on increasing productivity and technological development. Above all, and consistent with all this, the necessity for federal co-operation will be a must.
These are but a few of the corner-stones which I would like to elaborate upon further. Unfortunately, time does not permit.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to address particularly the neglect of the forest industry by this Government and, of course, since I come from British Columbia, I am particularly concerned about the consequences of that neglect.
The Minister who just spoke said that most of the promises had been carried out, including forestry. I do not know what he had in mind. As I look at the promises, I see that on July 5, 1984 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in Prince Albert that a Conservative Government would "recognize the
Supply
overwhelming economic importance of the forest industry". In their election handbook and in other speeches which the Prime Minister gave, they promised to "establish a new department of forestry at the federal level". We all cheered that because we thought, considering that this was Canada's largest export and the importance it had for all exports, that the neglect of the forest industry by previous Governments would at last be redressed. One of the most important ways in which it could be redressed would be to have a line department, not just a Minister of State, in Ottawa which would have as its full responsibility the development of the forest industry, silviculture, reforestation, and forest management in Canada.
We have been waiting since 1984 for a full department of forestry to be developed. All we got was a Minister of State for Forestry who has no real clout either in Cabinet, because he does not have a full department, or in the country. Indeed, the role he might have played on behalf of forestry has been even further diminished by the fact that he is also Minister of State for Mines. He has a dual role, and the mining industry is in about as bad a shape as the forest industry and probably needs fuller attention from the federal Government than it has been given. When the Government talks about having carried out its election promises, including the forestry field, I must ask why we still do not have a full-fledged department of forestry at the federal level.
The reports we have been receiving recently on the forest industry particularly in British Columbia are alarming, to put it mildly. I should like to refer to the most recent report a couple of months ago of the forest economics and policy analysis project of the University of British Columbia under Peter Pearse and written by Sten Nilsson. He pointed out in the report that unless immediate steps were taken to revitalize the forest industry, B.C. was 15 years away from an economic disaster. The report warned that there would be few, if any, plywood mills in the province and that the production of lumber, pulp, and newsprint would decline seriously. It also indicated that nearly 7,000 more direct jobs would disappear, that is, on top of the 17,000 or more direct jobs which have already disappeared in the forest industry.
He also pointed out in the study that the annual volume of timber available in B.C., which is now about 75 million cubic metres, would decline to 67 million cubic metres and, even with productivity improvements, it would mean a 5 per cent to 10 per cent decline in pulp and a 5 per cent drop in lumber. The report went on to indicate that the timber volume could dip as low as 44 million cubic metres with catastrophic results.
As I mentioned a moment ago, the report indicated that most plywood plants in B.C. would close by the year 2000, and that a switch from bulk commodity products to greater value added products was necessary. However, we see very little movement in that direction.
Most significant of all is that the report indicates that the industry needs to invest $35 billion by the year 2000 in reforestation and modernization but that it "cannot generate

March 23, 1987
Supply
sufficient capital". This is perhaps the most serious component in the picture of the B.C. forest industry.
I mentioned a moment ago the unemployment which has already taken place in the forest industry and that the UBC report projected that it would continue at an accelerating rate. Returning for a moment to the promises of the Government, it promised jobs, jobs, jobs. I assume that meant jobs in western Canada and in eastern Canada-indeed, in all parts of Canada. It is absolutely incredible that the unemployment rate in British Columbia is now running at 13.3 per cent, seasonally adjusted, as opposed to a national average of 9.6 per cent.
Let us look at some of the areas of the province in detail. We see that unemployment is running at about 18 per cent in the Kootenays; at about 17 per cent to 18 per cent in the interior, in the Okanagan and Kamloops; at over 12 per cent on Vancouver Island; at 14 per cent in Prince George and the northern interior; and, perhaps one of the most amazing statistics of all, at 14 per cent in the lower mainland, greater Vancouver. In fact, in February of this year it was 14.3 per cent, the highest unemployment in any major metropolitan centre. Youth unemployment in British Columbia is running at 22 per cent. There have not been jobs, jobs, jobs.
Some of us at least hoped that as a result of the federal Government's export tax on softwood lumber in the deal worked out with American lumber producers, a deal we questioned very much at the time, the revenue, which in the case of B.C. would amount to between $360 million and $400 million per year, would go into silviculture, reforestation, and the adjustment needs of workers. We hoped that it would be at last a shot in the arm to the forest industry. The Government, in the creation of the Canada-B.C. Forest Resource Development Agreement, will actually pump in $18 million this year, which will be matched by B.C. When we saw what would be the results of the federal export tax on softwood lumber in revenues, it seemed to many of us on this side of the House that at last some genuine effort could be or would be made to see to the redevelopment of the forest industry.
It was extremely disappointing, as I stated on Friday in the House, to discover that the British Columbia Government was putting only $36 million in new money into silviculture, reforestation, and so on. I know that it has been indicated in the Budget and in some of the speeches of the B.C. Minister of Finance that the amount is $54 million. As I mentioned, $18 million of that is the part that would automatically be going into forestry under the Canada-B.C. Forest Resource Development Agreement-that $18 million is not new money that could have come out of the federal export tax-leaving only $36 million. Yet, as I say, the export tax on softwood will bring somewhere between $360 million and $400 million. No wonder the British Columbia Government was able to cut its deficit. It simply put what we firmly believe are federal moneys, it is a federal tax, into general revenues in order to do other things and reduce the deficit. The response to this activity by the Socred Government from the forest industry itself has been extremely critical.
In last Friday's Vancouver Sun we find;-
Spokesmen for both management and labour said they are "disappointed" that more revenue from the $350 million tax on softwood lumber exports to the U.S. is not going directly into silviculture.
The harshest critic of the reforestation plan was International Woodworkers of America Regional President Jack Munro, who said the provincial Government has failed to live up to its responsibility to B.C.'s primary engine of economic growth.
"There could be all kinds of jobs in the forest industry, not just silviculture and reforestation, but secondary industries, manufacturing, products that haven't even been thought of yet," Munro said.
He said the revenues earned from the lumber-export tax should have been invested more heavily in the forest industry.
"We don't have enough nurseries, we don't have enough trees, and in the nurseries we do have they're shutting down," Munro said.
Mike Apsey, president of the Council of Forest Industries of B.C., also expressed regret the provincial Government did not commit more funds from the exports revenue to reforestation.
"If there is a disappointment, that's it," Apsey said. "All of the forestry community in this province has been recommending some sort of fund be set up into which the export tax proceeds would be put."
Art Gruntman, vice-president of the Canadian Paperworkers Union said putting most of the $350 million into general revenue instead of reforestation is "utterly and totally wrong."
I think the people of B.C. have the right to expect that the major part of the export tax money be put into reforestation because it has got to be done. We are running out of trees."
The point in quoting these sources in the forest industry, Madam Speaker, is that they say they expect to see a large part, if not all, of the revenues from the export tax on softwood going into the forest industry. That was certainly the expectation of the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) who herself, on February 5, referred to British Columbia as a silvicultural slum. Surely it you want to remedy the situation, if you want to see a development in forestry and if you want to try to curb the growth of unemployment in the forest industry sector, then you, the federal Government, when federal money is going into the province, should have required some performance guarantee. The federal Government should have at least said in a written agreement with the province, and with the other provinces as well that receive revenues from the export tax, that x amount of money will go to the forest industry.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister said on Friday that that would be dictating. The federal Government, when it is spending federal moneys, whether in health care or, in the old days, in post-secondary education, sets guidelines for the expenditure by the provinces of those moneys. I do not hear people objecting and saying that this is dictating if it is in the field of health care, which presumably, according to the BNA Act, is a field of provincial jurisdiction. Yet somehow or other the Conservative Party is saying, "You cannot have some kind of performance guarantee on the expenditure of revenues from a federal export tax". That is absolutely ridiculous, Madam Speaker. As I said on Friday, the Prime Minister has been conned, taken, by Premier Vander Zalm who is laughing all the way to the bank as he uses these moneys for other purposes or to cut his deficit.
March 23, 1987

1 am reminded very much of the comparable situation in post-secondary education. Elon. Members well know that until the Liberal Government, supported by the Tory Opposition, changed the rules a decade ago, the moneys sent from the federal Government to the provincial Governments for postsecondary education under the fiscal arrangements Act had to be spent on post-secondary education. Since then the provinces can spend that money any way they please.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to speak in response to the motion of my friend from Yorkton-Melville. The motion condemns the Government for its lack of what he calls a long-term economic development strategy for western Canada. Perhaps the Hon. Member should consult his constituents as to whether they condemn a Government which dismantled the much hated National
March 23, 1987

Energy Program of the previous Government, removed the PGRT, and abolished the universally unpopular Foreign Investment Review Act. The Government has launched as well trade negotiations with the U.S. which stand to benefit western Canada. This Government does indeed have in place a longterm economic development strategy for western Canada. That strategy is based on the principle that the economic health of western Canada, as does the rest of the country, depends on private sector led initiatives.
For this Government regional economic development stands at the centre of economic policy. We regard it as part of the process of building a greater, more cohesive pan-Canadian community. It is no less an exercise in nation-building in this century than was the construction of the railways in the last century. We will all remember that only a week ago in this House the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) underscored the role that regional development plays in the economic thinking of this Government. He warned against the danger of building two Canadas, one which is rich and promising and one which is underdeveloped and underemployed. He went on to speak about the need for building one Canada where fairness and equality of opportunity for all would prevail.
The basic principles of that policy were enunciated in the Throne Speech of October, 1986. That speech called for new approaches which would build on the human and natural resources strength of the regions and which would show greater sensitivity to local conditions and opportunities. In a very few words those are the corner-stones of our new directions in regional development policy.
I am pleased to note that the New Democratic Party, in its March, 1987, convention in Montreal seems to have endorsed this approach. It approved a shifting of priority for regional development away from a complete reliance on investment from outside the regions to a more self-reliant approach emphasizing the application of human and physical capital already in less developed regions. I appreciate the NDP support for our policy.
The type of assistance the federal Government provides to assist these aims can take many forms. That is why we provided, for example, $263 million of federal support to Expo 86, for example. That is why as well the Government is providing one-third support to the $50 million Yellowhead Highway upgrading program. Let us talk now about specifics and the instruments we have available to deliver these regional programs.
First, the Government has in place a very effective instrument for economic development in the western provinces in our ERDA agreements which we negotiate with the provincial Governments. The ERDAs allow for agreed approaches to priority areas pertaining to the provinces. Each ERDA outlines a broad development strategy and priorities for action. The agreement forms the framework for the development of specific subsidiary agreements tailored to the needs of each region. Since September, 1984, my Department has committed $308 million under 16 subsidiary agreements with the western
Supply
provinces, and a further $93 million under agreements that were part of the previous agreement system.

In Manitoba for example, Madam Speaker, subsidiary agreements have been concluded with respect to the development of an urban bus transit system, the launching of a tourism initiative, an another project for downtown Winnipeg, as my colleague would know. Similar agreements with Saskatchewan will pave the way for new technological industries and their rapid expansion. By the same token, Madam Speaker, this will promote the tourism industry in the province and boost economic development in northern Saskatchewan.
In addition, last year in Alberta for instance, we signed a few agreements concerning science and technology, native people, economic development, and transport. The Department shares the cost of a number of tourism, farm technology, and northern development subsidiary agreements. In British Columbia, several such agreements are aimed at promoting tourism, industry and small business. Regional and economic development agreements are the key to future growth. But, Madam Speaker, they are not the only program designed to improve western diversification and economic expansion. The main objective of this program is to promote industrial and regional development through private sector projects designed for just such expansion. The industries and new technologies which stand a very good chance of becoming profitable are also included in these projects so that we may be able to guarantee the sustained development of a region while at the same time remaining competitive on international markets.

The program responds specifically to the needs of the small and medium-sized businesses and compliments other federal programs. Since September, 1984, assistance has been authorized of close to $100 million for some 470 projects in western Canada. More than 63 per cent of this assistance as well was authorized for innovation, expansion and modernization projects. Then there is the Western Transportation Industrial Development Program. This program was specifically tailored to the four western provinces to provide assistance for firms in the manufacturing, processing and other related industries so that they might take advantage of opportunities presented by changes in freight rate legislation.
It was under our Government that we expanded the benefit of this program to assist Alberta. Since September, 1984, as well, 161 authorizations have been made under this program representing $29 million in assistance.
Under the Small Businesses Loans Act, since the beginning of 1984, nearly 24,000 business enterprises have been assisted in the western provinces to obtain term loans to a total of about $670 million. These small businesses have access to term loans at better rates for acquisition and modernization of equipment and buildings. They are engaged in manufacturing, wholesale trades, retail, services, construction, transportation

March 23, 1987
Adjournment Debate
and communication. Also, since 1984 the Federal Business Development Bank has provided term loans to western Canada, as it did to eastern Canada, in response to the question of my colleague, to promote and assist in the establishment and development of fitness enterprises.
The list goes on. The very popular special Agricultural and Rural Development Act program has provided $54 million in assistance for western Canada since September, 1984, primarily to native and native-related initiatives. The Native Economic Development Program has provided another $47 million to native peoples' business initiatives. The Government is fully committed to helping native people in Canada achieve economic self-reliance and will make this program as effective as possible to help realize this objective.
Recently announced improvements to the native program include widening program criteria to enable primary resource businesses to qualify for assistance, broadening program support for community economic development activity, improving program accessibility and delivery, creating new flexibility for individual applicants, and extending the deadlines for applications by one year to March 31, 1989. These are not just statistics, Madam Speaker. These funds are being provided to support dynamic, exciting initiatives.
I have mentioned these federal initiatives because I want to underscore the broad policy and program directions that the Government has set in terms of encouraging the kind of local entrepreneurship that is needed to promote regional selfreliance. The Government will continue to use the traditional tools of development that have worked. There is clearly a need to continue to strengthen the resource base and to ensure as well that the necessary infrastructure for development is in place. This is reflected in the approach the Government has taken with initiatives under the economic and regional development agreements with the provinces.
The Government is also sensitive to the changes which have taken place in the West. For this reason I have agreed to review our programs and ensure that they are regionally sensitive. In the West this will mean focusing on diversifying the resource base that exists. A perfect example would be the recent signing of a Memorandum of Understanding with the Province of British Columbia on the Pacific Centre for Trade, Commerce and Travel. This MOU will allow the two Governments to co-ordinate initiatives to enhance British Columbia's future economic development.
These include encouraging the growth of international banking and other financial services in Vancouver, coordinating transportation improvements, enhancing trade-related services and opportunities in those professional and technical services where British Columbians have developed significant expertise. The MOU will also improve the coordination of marketing and promotion of British Columbia as a tourist destination. This is only a sample of long-term economic planning which the Government believes in.
Partnership in development is essential if we are to succeed in strengthening the ability of all our regions to meet the challenges and opportunities of the emerging world economy. Aggressive international competition in resource and traditional manufacturing industries represents one such challenge. Rapid growth in services and knowledge-intensive industries represent new opportunities. The development efforts required to enhance the productivity of our traditional wealth-generating industries and to foster these skills and knowledge necessary to capture the new opportunities can only be undertaken in close co-operation with the provinces. Their jurisdictional responsibilities for resource management and many facets of social policy mean that the provinces have a key role to play in the development effort.
I have launched a joint review with my provincial counterparts to determine what direction our future collaborative approach to regional development should take where joint programs exist. Provincial Ministers and I will be looking for realistic and practical ways to engage the Canadian people of all regions in their economic development. I am optimistic about our prospects for arriving at a consensus about what needs to be done and how to develop initiatives that are sensitive to the unique circumstances of each region.
The Government's broad directions have been set. Other initiatives announced in last fall's Throne Speech, specifically the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and western diversification, will also reflect these broad directions. As was stated in the Speech from the Throne, the Government is convinced many positive proposals for new policy initiatives will come from those who live and work in the regions concerned.
Those words sum up my message today, Madam Speaker. This is not a Government which believes in made-in-Ottawa solutions. Ultimately the solutions have to be found in the regions and in the spirit of self-reliance and initiative of the Canadian people.

speechtext: What about an elected Senate?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
There were two resolutions for an elected Senate with equal representation from each province, one put forward by the Liberal Association of New Brunswick and another by the Liberal Party in Manitoba. Both those resolutions carried by wide margins in the Liberal Party. Let me say that in the last Parliament, before the election of 1984, we had a special joint committee of the House and the Senate to discuss and study Senate reform. I appeared before that committee and recommended an elected Senate with equal representation in all provinces. I did that as a representative from Quebec. I have come to realize, having been here for 22 years, that we will never have federal institutions which do justice to the regions of Canada which are less populated unless we have a Senate which is elected and which counterbalances the "rep by pop" principle in the House of Commons.
I think westerners realize that, unfortunately, they will continue to be short-changed as long as we have a federal legislative system where the overwhelming bulk of votes in this House are in the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec. If one Party gets together and gets those votes in Ontario and Quebec, it controls the country. The only way to counterbalance that sort of situation is to have an elected Senate as there is in the United States with an equal number of seats from each province so that we then counterbalance the strong populations in Ontario and Quebec with an upper house which is effective and can really represent the people in those provinces. I am committed to that kind of policy. We will then have policies coming out of the central Government which will more truly reflect and help all the regions of this country.
There were just two of the resolutions which were carried by the Liberal Party which were directed to the needs of the West. There were others dealing with full employment policies and with policies related to a western industrial strategy. A resolution was introduced by the Saskatchewan Liberal Association to the effect that we establish a western industrial strategy to develop secondary industries, particularly those related to the resource and agricultural industries, and to
develop and support infrastructures to that end. There is more detail to it, but resolutions along those lines were also passed in the areas of energy, agriculture and other economic matters of interest to the West.
This motion states that the Government should be condemned for its lack of policy for the West, and I fully support that condemnation. The policy of the Government has been one of laissez-faire, if we let the private sector do it, the job will get done. The job is not getting done. The rate of unemployment is going up in Alberta and in British Columbia. It is still quite low in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, but both provinces have had a decline in their labour market which accounts for their continuing low rate. There has been a migration over the years from those two provinces but not to the same extent from Alberta and British Columbia. A policy of laissez-faire, let the private sector do it, will not work in Canada. It has never worked in Canada. What we require is a sound partnership with the private sector between Governments at all levels. I do not go to the extent of the New Democratic Party which would like to see a dominant role played by the Government. We have seen in this country under Liberal Governments over the years sound partnerships between the federal Government and provincial Governments with the private sector. Our country is so vast, with sparse population in many places and many regional problems, but when that partnership came together we had, as I pointed out, low rates of unemployment, high rates of growth and economic justice for Canadians in all parts of the country.
I support this motion. I believe that more can be done. 1 believe that instead of budgets being cut in the Department of Employment and Immigration, there should be an increase at this time, especially in those provinces where there are increasing rates of unemployment. Instead of cuts in the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion there should be increases. Some of the things mentioned by the Minister are good things, but that is not enough. More has to be done. We need more political will, more commitment from the Government, if those problems are going to be solved in the West as well as in the East.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to the motion of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), a member whose provincial ridings are now fully represented by provincial Progressive Conservative members.
