subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext: It is for sure that he will need some. It is interesting to note that we come from a perspective in western Canada where for years and years we went without any federal representation. All we had in the federal Cabinet were a couple of broken-down Senators who were wandering around the countryside shrugging off responsibility for decisions of the previous Government, occasionally accepting whatever gratitude there was for some lucky international incident that might have resulted in something good for the west. But by and large, there was no representation whatever. I am happy to note now that western Canada is fully represented in a national Cabinet by some 58 Members of Parliament, 10 Ministers, among them the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) and a number of others. I am heartened by that because it is fairly evident that a considerable response is being made to western Canada, the likes of which has not been seen in our history.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext: We agree with that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
In dealing with this motion, it is important to do so from the perspective that we in western Canada will never be the manufacturing, the industrial centre of Canada, nor for that matter the population centre. We should not approach it from that point of view because there will not be the fundamental changes suddenly making us a country of 100 million people. What is important are the steps that have been taken in western Canada by the Government to strengthen and to diversify what we have.
I would like to speak to this motion from the perspective of the agricultural sector as a representative of a prairie riding which is largely dependent upon the growing of wheat. Contrary to what is stated in the motion, the Government has acted and continues to act in support of the important sector of agriculture. The member who proposed this motion should be
March 23, 1987

well aware of our Government's high priority commitment to agriculture. That, of course, includes a commitment to the grain farmers in western Canada. Agriculture matters to each and every Canadian. Our grain industry means jobs, exports and the very survival of a great many rural communities in western Canada. The federal Government's many policies and programs are proof of our commitment to a strong agricultural industry in western Canada. We are addressing the hardships currently threatening many of our western grain farmers.
I would like to repeat what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said in a debate here last week, "That this Government will stack its record in agriculture, including programs that benefit western farmers, against the record of any previous Government". I challenge anyone to take an objective look at the record and to make the comparison. The initiatives and the dollars tell the story.
To begin with, it would be worthwhile for all Members of this Elouse to examine the roots of the problems facing farmers in western Canada. The problems are not simple, nor are the solutions. First, we have to acknowledge that over the past couple of decades farmers have made great advances by applying new technologies. Our grain farmers have become more efficient and more productive. Those are positive developments, but they have implications. We should consider also that many farmers in western Canada are carrying debtloads many times what they were carrying 15 years ago. Some of that was, I think, government induced. We had the business investment tax credit, an ill-advised Liberal initiative, which encouraged many farmers to overinvest in expensive farm machinery and equipment and to go into debt for it. We had high-priced land, and 1 hate to say that in the Province of Saskatchewan the stimulus and impetus for some of that was the Land Bank Program of the New Democratic Party's provincial Government of the day, a Government which used young farmers own tax money to enter in bidding wars over the value of land, a most unfortunate circumstance.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext: It was lower than the markets.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-WESTERN CANADA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
Much of the increase occurred in the 1970s when farmers borrowed heavily for equipment and farmlands to expand their operations. Those expansions left many farmers in western Canada with high-debt costs and monthly payments that are very hard to meet.
The high interest rates of the early 1980s continue to haunt many farmers who are still trying to recover. In addition, the value of farmland has fallen in western Canada, eroding equity, and making it difficult for farmers to borrow operating capital. All of these factors are influencing farm incomes. Obviously, no single program can address the wide range of problems. The international market-place is also a major influence, probably the most significant influence of all on our western grain farmers. Some traditional customers for our grain exports have become net exporters themselves. Surpluses have built up around the world. Some countries are trying to
Supply
get rid of their surpluses by offering huge export subsidies. The European Economic Community and the United States are the most notable examples. This subsidy war has driven world prices way down. Our grain farmers in western Canada are among the unfortunate victims of this trade war.
The federal Government recognizes that these international influences must be dealt with at the international level. We are doing that vigorously, forcefully and on a priority basis. I would be remiss if 1 did not comment on the efforts of the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) who has been instrumental in getting together representatives of the grain exporting countries with a view to trying to bring back some measure of sanity into the international wheat market-place.
It is interesting to note that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister for International Trade succeeded in having agriculture included for the first time as a priority item in the forthcoming Uruguay round of GATT talks. The Government knows that solutions to the international problems will not happen overnight. We also know that the problems facing farmers in western Canada are the result of many different influences. That is why we must approach the solutions, not from one but from many angles, and that is exactly what we are doing.
Our Government has delivered an historic special grains program, a program that no other Government has ever matched. It is a program that demonstrates clearly the Government's understanding of the problems facing the nation's grain farmers. The Special Canadian Grains Program is putting $1 billion in cash directly into the pockets of about
200,000	grain and oil seed farmers this year. The share of this program accruing to producers within my Province of Saskatchewan is in excess of $400 million. The net farm income in Saskatchewan this year was projected to be possibly $400 million. With one stroke of the pen our Government has managed to double the net farm income in the Province of Saskatchewan this year. I am disappointed that there are those representing western Canada who would have the temerity in the face of that to suggest that our Government has not addressed agricultural hardship.
The special grains program is specifically designed to help cushion the drop in grain prices caused by the massive export subsidies in the European Economic Community and the United States. The Government worked with farm leaders and organizations, including the prairie pools and some 30 others to put together a fair and equitable program for distributing the $1 billion among grain producers. I would like to point out that about 84 per cent of this $1 billion will be going to grain farmers in western Canada. In fact, about 140,000 cheques worth one-quarter of a billion dollars were mailed to eligible Canadian Wheat Board permit holders in January and February. We expect that about $600 million of the remaining $700 million to be paid out under the Special Canadian Grains Program will go to farmers in western Canada. It is largely because of this special program that payments made to

March 23, 1987
Supply
western grain farmers under federal programs in 1987 will far exceed any previous level at any time in this country's history.
The Special Canadian Grains Program, Madam Speaker, is not the only initiative that the Government has directed toward western agriculture. We have the Federal-Provincial Crop Insurance Program, 50 per cent of which is contributed by the federal Government and 50 per cent by the producers, with the cost of administration contributed by the participating provinces. This program has seen improved levels of coverage at no additional cost to the producer.
The Government also participates in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund making contributions of $2 for every $1 contributed by the western grain farmer. The Government has responded to representations from western grain farmers and delivered amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act in order to ensure that timely interim payments be made each spring. Under the western grain stabilization program, over $500 million was paid out in 1985, some $859 million last year and payments for the 1987 year will likely set a record. Western grain farmers can obviously expect a large interim payment again this year and very soon.
The Government also delivered two new lending programs to the Farm Credit Corporation, programs which are giving farmers more financial flexibility at a time when they really need it. Today, loans under the commodity-based loan program and the shared-risk programs total more than $300 million.
The Government amended the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act to double the level of cash advances and also to eliminate the irritant of having a landlord's signature required for a tenant to be able to secure advances. We delivered farm debt review boards which are helping farmers in western Canada to negotiate arrangements with their creditors, arrangements that will keep them on the land. So far, well over half of the arrangements that have been negotiated should result in keeping viable farms in operation.
We have also acted to reduce effectively farm input costs. Fast year, the Farm Fuel Tax Rebate Program reduced input costs for farmers by some $70 million. In this year's federal Budget, the rebate program was expanded to cushion farmers fully against the one-cent per litre tax increase on gas and diesel fuel. These rebates now total in excess of eight cents a litre or some 35 cents a gallon.
The $80 million interest rate reduction program continues to hold down interest costs for more than 5,000 farmers with Farm Credit Corporation loans. This five-year program is helping farmers who were caught by high interest rates in the early 1980s before we came into office and brought those rates down. Our economic policies have caused interest rates to drop by more than 4 percentage points so far. Every one point decline represents a saving to the farm community of between $100 million and $200 million. There is approximately $25
billion in farm debt outstanding, and it is easy to extrapolate from that just how important each 1 per cent reduction in interest rates really is.
Federal Government spending to benefit the grain farmers of western Canada and farmers in other parts of Canada as well is higher than it has ever been before. This year, the level will be much higher than last year's record level. Some of this assistance obviously comes from programs to which farmers contribute, programs on which I have touched already, but the bulk of it, particularly this year, represents federal funds. That is over and above spending on important and ongoing programs that serve the farm community such as research, technology, inspection, grading and trade development. The level of direct payments to farmers is high and will no doubt remain high until market prices recover. We know, however, that this investment in agriculture is a worth-while investment on behalf of all Canadians.
There can be absolutely no doubt about the Government's commitment to western grain farmers and indeed to farmers all across Canada. We have delivered and we will continue to deliver. The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board are continuing to meet with their provincial counterparts and with farm leaders to plan new measures that will benefit western grain farmers in the future. Agriculture continues to be a key element of the Government's agenda for economic renewal. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled a progress report on the agenda along with his February Budget, spelling out the Government's commitment to having the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board continue to meet with farm organizations and the provinces on a priority basis.
The Government's objective is to find new ways to ensure that the Canadian grain industry remains a competitive force in world markets. In fact, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board met with farm leaders on March 5 to begin planning actions to assist grain farmers in the coming crop year. Obviously it is still too soon to come to any definitive conclusions about what help will be needed or how it should be delivered, but it is clear, and farm leaders have agreed, that grain farmers should not expand or shift production on the expectation of the special payment based on this year's acreage or production. Any new assistance measures will be production and market neutral.
The Minister of Agriculture will be meeting with his provincial counterparts next week on March 30 and with farm leaders again in May or June. Western grain farmers and other farmers from coast to coast recognize that the Government regards agriculture as a top priority. They appreciate the fact that we intend to include the farm community in the planning of future actions.
The Government's record speaks for itself. It is unequalled. We take a back seat to no one in actions on behalf of western grain farmers. While others may talk, we have taken strong, concrete and significant action. Just as we have taken action in
March 23, 1987

the past, we will continue to take action in the future, in good faith and on behalf of western Canada's farmers.
It is unfortunate that the motion has been put forward in such a negative fashion. It is a pity that it is always the dark side and the gloom and doom that seems to be coming from the benches of the NDP. In fact, there is a lot of hope out there and promise for the future. There are good things happening and I want to refer to some recent figures which indicate, for example, that employment in Canada has increased between September, 1984, and February, 1987, by 719,000. That means that 719,000 more people are working today than just two and a half years ago. The bank rate is now at 7.14 per cent. That is more than five points lower than it was in September, 1984. The prime rate is down four and one-quarter points.
It is pretty clear that the greatest gift any Government can give to Canadians, whether in farm communities, in western Canada or in any walk of life anywhere in the country, is lower interest rates. It is pretty clear that the policies of the Government over-all have led to a very, very substantial drop in interest rates, and I think it is evident that the additional investment and jobs flowing from it have been forthcoming.
I was amazed at the remarks of the previous speaker who seemed to indicate that it was the job of Government to create jobs. I would categorically reject that proposition and suggest that it is the job of Government instead to create the conditions and the environment in which small business can flourish, in which entrepreneurs can invest capital with some reasonable hope of success without being weighed down by undue interest rates. Certainly it is through the small business sector that jobs are being created. They are being created because of the policies of the Government regarding small business in western Canada and everywhere else and because of the life-time capital gains tax exemption which gives some hope for small business people to be able in fact to realize their equity out of their businesses after lifetimes of hard work.
In answer to my hon. friend's motion, I would suggest that he should ask Canadians where they would prefer to be. Would they prefer to be in Canada or would they prefer to be in some other country? Perhaps we should look at the flip side of that and ask why it is that people from virtually every nation on the face of the earth are trying by the thousands to get into Canada by any means possible. They are prepared to leave behind everything they have in order to get into Canada. In conclusion, I want to say that I am glad to be a Canadian, I am glad to be a western Canadian, and I am glad to be a western Canadian under this Government.

The Minister of Agriculture has already indicated, in response to questions in this House and elsewhere, that farmers ought not to plan production based on the criteria everyone used in this special grains program. He also indicated, and I am sure the Hon. Member knows this, that there are ongoing consultations between the Minister and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, as well as with representatives of many farm organizations, with a view to assessing the situation and determining the appropriate response for the forthcoming year. I am sure that in doing that they will make reference to the international prices and the sort of export activity, subsidies elsewhere, and the pressures bearing on the farm community. The Hon. Member can rest assured that this Government will continue to make a generous and understanding response to the problems facing farmers, especially the hard hit grain farmers.
As to whether the form of assistance could be along the lines he posed in his question, that is some sort of a guaranteed price equivalent to what it was during the past crop year or some other level, I believe that remains to be seen. It is clear that there are those who would criticize that approach by saying that it might encourage a shifting into wheat, for example, as a result of an artificially high price. I am sure there are those in the farm community who would say that this is not the way to go. We ought not to be encouraging that at this time, rather, we ought to be encouraging the farmers with programs which address input costs and interest rates. Clearly there are literally hundreds and hundreds of proposals being discussed. I know they are being discussed in my riding among farmers everywhere, in the coffee shops, homes and halls. I think, too, that the same discussions are being held nationally. We know that the programs to be put forward, if need be, will be the proper response and will take into account the needs of Canadian producers as well as the financial ability of the Government to respond.
If I might briefly address the second point, I believe the Hon. Member asked if I would prefer to see a freeze on freight rates. I am not a transportation expert by any means. Privately, of course I would. I was under the impression that those rates were set by formula and by statute, which statute was put forward by the Hon. Member's Party some years ago. I would think he would be able to answer that question better than I.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the list is long but I will try to be brief. I think there have been enormous strides made toward diversification in western Canada. In answer to my hon. friend I would like to refer to a couple of matters in Saskatchewan. Presently the second largest paper mill in Canada, which will produce 600 new jobs, is being built in the Prince Albert area. An ERDA agreement has been signed between Saskatchewan and the federal Government which will cause $100 million to be spent in the irrigation sector in Saskatchewan. The Government of Canada has guaranteed $250 million to $300 million worth of loans to assist in the new Regina upgrader project. This is the largest project of its kind in Canada at the present time. It will upgrade Saskatchewan heavy and medium crude oil which will give us an opportunity to refine these products at home in Saskatchewan.
In my own City of Swift Current, Saskatchewan, in the first three months of this year there are already four times as many applications for building permits as there were in the entire previous year. There is a mall project going ahead there which has been talked about for years and is finally coming to fruition, notwithstanding low farm and oil prices. It is coming into play now because of low interest rates and the outstanding economic policies of the Government.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. The first sentence of the motion before us reads:
That this House condemns the government for its lack of a long term economic
development strategy for Western Canada that would, among other things-
March 23, 1987

It goes on to deal with the agricultural sector, the forest industry, the energy sector and the need for economic diversification in western Canada. The motion before the House condemns the Government for its lack of a long-term economic development strategy for Canada. I would like to put my opinion with regard to this motion and the poor performance of the Government on the record in the few minutes which are available to me today.
To put it briefly, I think the Government has simply forgotten western Canada. I will give you three reasons why I think that is the case. I want to discuss three aspects of western economic development. I want to discuss briefly the political promises which the Conservatives made when they were seeking office, particularly those promises made to western Canada. I want to discuss what is actually going on in western Canada today and I want to take a brief look at the Government's economic policies.
If 1 can have the attention of the House, Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by pointing out that when the Conservatives were running for office they promised "jobs, jobs, jobs". They promised to make a place around the Cabinet table for western Canada. They promised to bring western Canada in from the cold with regard to power and decision-making. Those were the promises, but what has been the result, what kind of performance has the Government put on? It has certainly been a performance in the theatrical sense, but with regard to the promise of "jobs, jobs, jobs", as indicated in an article in The Globe and Mail of February 28, the jobs which have been created have been created in Ontario and not in western Canada. The article by Ross Howard says:
Between January, 1986, and January of this year, the total number of jobs in
the country rose by 137,000, according to unadjusted figures. But only 5,000
of those jobs were created outside Ontario.
The article also says that:
-more than 95 per cent of the additional jobs created last year were located
in one province-Ontario.
The promise of "jobs, jobs, jobs" has been real for the Golden Horseshoe of Ontario, but it has been a lie for western Canada. The jobs which were promised by the Government have not been created in western Canada. What has been the result of the promise to include western Canadians in the economic decision-making of the country? Briefly, the result has been that farmers are in difficulty today due to the performance of the Government. Small Canadian oil companies in Alberta are endangered due to the performance of the Government. Support is rising throughout western Canada for the western separatist Party as a result of the actions of the Government. Even more ludicrous is the fact that the Government has revived support in western Canada for the Liberal Party. That is an achievement, albeit a negative one. I hope the Liberal Party, stem and trunk, has not been revived, but it has certainly been revived in the public opinion polls.

We want an industrial policy and an economic strategy for western Canada. We want to be more than only hewers of wood and drawers of water. We want in on industrial development. We want our fair share of the economic pie and we expect the Government to live up to its promises made when it was running for public office. March 23, 1987
Adjournment Debate

Madam Speaker, this evening I have a question for you. Do you believe in polls? I do not mean telephone poles or hydro poles, or even barber poles. I mean public opinion polls. I can tell, Madam Speaker, that like me, there are probably one or two recent polls in which you would rather not believe. However, I believe in public opinion polls and I suspect that you do as well.
Recently there were two public opinion polls on the question of acid rain. Those polls found that two out of five Canadians believe that reaching an acid rain agreement with the United States is even more important than reaching a trade agreement with the United States, as far as Canada is concerned.
Acid rain comes from emissions that originate from coal-fired smelters, from non-ferrous smelters like the Inco smelter, and emissions from automobiles. These emissions float into the air, seem to go a long distance, and come down to have a devastating effect on our environment. We know that these emissions cause damage to fish, birds, lakes, trees and to buildings all around us.
At least half of these emissions emanate from the United States. It is no wonder that Canadians are concerned about these acid rain emissions and getting some sort of agreement with the United States to solve the acid rain problem. In the same poll to which I referred, 60 per cent of Canadians who responded indicated that they felt our Government was not doing enough about getting an agreement with the United States on acid rain.
That prompted me to think about just what the Government has done about acid rain since it came to office in the last two and a half years. It made me think back to the fact that in January, 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated that Canada could not expect to make any progress with the United States in its negotiations unless we came to the negotiating table with clean hands and unless we got our own house in order.
In February, 1985, I remember that the federal and provincial Environment Ministers came together to agree on some targets to achieve the goal of reducing sulphur dioxide emissions in eastern Canada by some 50 per cent of their 1980 levels by the year 1994. The federal Government agreed to put up financial assistance, as did the provinces, to help those smelters ensure that they could meet those targets and reduce those acid rain emissions.
I also remember that in March, 1985, the Prime Minister announced a national program for reducing acid rain emissions in Canada. That included new automobile emission standards, $150 million for smelter emission controls, $25 million for technology development, $70 million for cleaner and more efficient use of coal, $18 million a year for research and monitoring, and a study of the increased use of low sulphur western coal. All of that amounted at the time to a commitment of some $300 million on the part of the federal Government toward acid rain control in this country.
In March of that same year Hon. Members will remember that the Prime Minister met with President Reagan at the so-called Shamrock Summit. At that time they agreed to appoint acid rain envoys, Mr. Bill Davis, the former Premier of Ontario, and Mr. Drew Lewis, to study and identify ways of solving the problem.
In July of 1985 the federal Government announced new automobile emission standards that would be effective in September of this year. In January of last year the Special Envoys reported and recommended ways in which the United States could implement a five-year, $5 billion clean coal technology program. Then, in March of last year, President Reagan announced that he was endorsing that program. At the same time the Canadian Government announced that it was providing $9 million to assist the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, Inco and Falconbridge, to meet their deadlines for reducing acid rain emissions in this country. In March of this year you will recall, Madam Speaker, that the federal Government and the provinces began entering into formal abatement agreements. Hopefully, all of these agreements will be entered into soon.
Those are the steps that we have been taking in this country. What have the Americans been doing? Until recently, in fact just up until last week, it has been hard to see exactly what they have been doing. In fact, until last week they had no indication whatsoever of even putting money in their budget. Last week they announced they were going to do so. However, I heard the President of the United States on television last Thursday indicating that he still was not sure what the real problem was with acid rain. We are now coming to the point where it is up to Canada to meet with the United States, meet with President Reagan, to see what we can do about getting the Americans to finally get moving on this issue.
Tonight, I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that when our Prime Minister meets with President Reagan very shortly that he will give him an even bigger earful than he gave to Vice-President Bush just a few weeks ago.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Stewart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in March of 1986 President Reagan endorsed the Report of the Special Envoys on Acid Rain and their recommendations, as was just mentioned by the Hon. Member. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) took that as a commitment by the administration that acid rain was a serious transboundary problem and that it would seek the funds necessary to implement the Special Envoys' Report. The President's 1988 budget proposal submitted to Congress in January of this year provided the first concrete information on the U.S. response to the President's commitment.
The initiatives outlined in that budget proposal fell far short of meeting the commitments made to Canada by President Reagan. This was the clear message that the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and
March 23, 1987

the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) gave to Vice-President Bush at their meeting on January 21.
However, as recently as last week President Reagan announced several initiatives. These initiatives represent a significant and important step forward in our efforts to develop the bilateral accord that will provide a long-term, lasting solution to the acid rain problem. They will also put specific substance and timetable to the general commitments that he made at the 1986 summit meeting.
For instance, the administration will secure $500 million per year in new funds for each of the next five years to cost share clean coal commercial demonstration projects which meet the criteria of the Special Envoys. The projects will not be of a research nature but, rather, will be to demonstrate new cost-effective technologies on a commercial scale and to reduce the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide into eastern Canada. The projects to be funded under the program will be selected by a panel which will include Canadian government representatives. The administration is also examining its economic and regulatory programs to determine any disincentives that may exist to the implementation of pollution controls.
Reaching this agreement before the summit will allow the Prime Minister and President Reagan to discuss how to move the issue even further ahead at their next meeting. The Canadian objective is to get the United States to reduce its transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide into eastern Canada to about two million tonnes, about 50 per cent of the 1980 level, and to implement programs to achieve this level on a scheduled basis. This objective is based on sound scientific information and existing principles and obligations under international law that countries must ensure that activities within their jurisdiction do not cause damage to the environment of other countries.
The commitment to our objective holds strong. Acid rain will be one of the top agenda items at the April 6 summit meeting and we will do everything possible in the weeks leading to the summit to advance the issue.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-(A) LINGUISTIC POLICY- GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) MANNER IN WHICH POLICY IS APPLIED
CANADA POST CORPORATION-(A) LINGUISTIC POLICY- GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) MANNER IN WHICH POLICY IS APPLIED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention this evening concerns the linguistic policy of the Canada Post Corporation.
First, I would like to make something clear for all those who might be interested in this debate.
I personally believe in bilingual services whenever practical and possible. I am also very concerned about the linguistic problem, especially in Quebec, which can be a very emotional problem, as I know personally since I represent the constituency of Saint-Leonard-Anjou which was the scene of a well-publicized linguistic conflict a while back. I can therefore assure all my colleagues, Madam Speaker, that I have no intention of initiating a linguistic debate.
Adjournment Debate
What I want to show this evening is that the Canada Post Corporation is doing everything possible to reduce its staff, harass its customers and cause people to wonder whether or not Canada really has a postal service.
Now for the facts. I shall start with an official document of the Canada Post Corporation where we find, on page 5, under the title "Guidelines for the publication of press releases and instructions, Quebec Division":
Official languages
The Quebec Division having been identified by the Official languages Commissioner as a unilingual French Division, all press releases and instructions will be written in French only. The English version of these documents will be available on request.
However, it is essential that communications with the outside public be published in both official languages when the English-speaking segment represents at least 10 per cent of the total population.
Madam Speaker, according to the figures, the Englishspeaking population of Quebec City and the area is only 2.8 per cent. This guideline therefore applies.
At the beginning of December, as soon as Canada Post submitted its corporate plan, it immediately issued new directives, announcing that from now on, the Customer Services Division, and perhaps I should explain that this is a technical division and not one that deals directly with customers, would be a bilingual division. I have no quarrel with the fact that Canada Post is free to issue such directives and to switch its divisions around, provided, Madam Speaker, employees who had these jobs when the division was still considered unilingual French, are given the time and assistance they need to become bilingual.
Unfortunately, Canada Post did as follows: From now on, this is a bilingual division so you are redundant. If you want to reapply to get your job back, you will have to prove that you are bilingual and you will not be given the necessary time or resources to become bilingual.
Madam Speaker, I think this is an intolerable situation for Quebec City, where only 2.8 per cent of the population is English-speaking, and it is unacceptable also because the policy was effective the day after it was announced.
Madam Speaker, I put the question to the Minister, and I was very disappointed at his reply which was that as a Minister, he could hardly be expected to be involved in that kind of minute details of the Corporation's operations. However, it is not a minute detail but a fundamental issue, Madam Speaker. It seems we are always having trouble with Canada Post which takes measures and takes the kind of action which makes one wonder about the measure of intelligence involved. We saw that this weekend, when someone at Canada Post, instead of trying to improve customer services, took the time to write a letter to Members of this House, to send us ... , and I imagine Madam Speaker, you also received the same form letter. They wrote us a letter saying: You have had complaints from your ridings, and this is how to answer those complaints. Since when is a Member of the House going to let someone at Canada Post dictate the answers he should

March 23, 1987
Adjournment Debate
give to his constituents? Who do the people working for the Canada Post Corporation think they are, Madam Speaker? These are the reasons why I was very disappointed with the reply of the Minister. We have a Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation, and if he really is responsible for the Corporation, he should immediately deal with the problem and instruct Canada Post to serve the taxpayers properly. Leave the Members of Parliament alone; they know what to tell their own constituents. We have no need for a model letter telling us how to answer their questions. We also believe that the employees should be given a chance. This is a harassment policy. How can there be any peace in the service when every opportunity is used to create further conflict? Who pays in the end? It is the public, the people who need the service.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-(A) LINGUISTIC POLICY- GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) MANNER IN WHICH POLICY IS APPLIED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I shall try to reply to my colleague and to respond to his concerns.
The Canada Post Corporation must obey the laws of Canada in all its activities, which includes the interpretation of the Official Languages Act. About a month ago, certain media reported that a number of Canada Post Corporation employees in Quebec City had been judged surplus to requirements by corporate management because they were not bilingual and did not speak English. Such is not the case, Madam Speaker.
When the sales and customer services department in Quebec City was reorganized last December, there was absolutely no change for 13 positions. Nine other positions were reclassified in order to better reflect the additional duties added to those positions, also reflecting the requirements of the Official Languages Act. In the course of that reorganization, customer service representative positions were reclassified from grade 2 to grade 3. This means that Customer Sales Service was added to the duties of grade 2 positions, which come under Customer Service. The new grade 3 positions have become bilingual.
Since bilingualism is a required qualification for the new positions, the corporation has made available to the employees involved, free of charge, an intensive course.
In the meantime, those employees are still working for the corporation, which has decided to wait for those employees to complete their intensive courses before considering any application for the new positions.
This does not necessarily mean they will be appointed, but Canada Post Corporation will have made the effort. Linder the existing agreement with the union, any corporation employee must be allowed to apply for the newly created positions.
The corporation's Chairman, Mr. Sylvain Cloutier, has informed us that Canada Post is committed, over the coming months and years, to better identify its customers' linguistic preferences and to offer them additional bilingual counter and telephone services.
The corporation's service to the public takes into account first language data as established by Statistics Canada, by
census divisions. The corporation is now reprocessing those statistics and expects to have in hand more pertinent data on the language profile of all its postal communities. Management officials will thus be able to make more accurate forecasts of linguistic requirements concerning over-the-counter services.
Telephone service in both official languages is another major Canada Post objective, and this is why management are now re-examining their telephone network and, more specifically, the services available in their 25 customer service units. They are considering such technological breakthroughs in this field as might enable them to meet the demand for information in English and French throughout Canada. The plan now being developed by Canada Post should have an impact on all telephone directories from coast to coast as of the beginning of fiscal year 1987-88.
In the next few months, Canada Post senior officials will be urged to play a more active and direct role in defining specific official languages objectives. Canada Post will also make sure that senior officials keep a closer and more formal progress watch through employee appraisal reports.
Since these appraisal reports bear directly on remuneration and promotion opportunities, they are tantamount to applying the good old carrot and stick principle which has proved to be quite successful over centuries. I do not see why it would not work just as well at Canada Post.

subtopic: RAILWAYS-GRAIN FREIGHT RATES. (B) REQUEST FOR RETENTION OF FREEZE ON FREIGHT RATES
RAILWAYS-GRAIN FREIGHT RATES. (B) REQUEST FOR RETENTION OF FREEZE ON FREIGHT RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on February 16 I put a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), asking him to give a clear indication of what the Government was going to do with regard to grain freight rates for western farmers. As you know, farmers are suffering through one of the most difficult times in their history. In the last general election, the Government Party made a clear commitment to maintain the freeze on western grain freight rates charged to farmers until the farmers were better able to make larger payments for grain freight rates.
A report has now been passed from the Senior Grain Transportation Agency to the Canadian Transport Commission indicating that grain freight rates will rise from $6 to approximately $8.50 or $9 per tonne in the coming crop year. Last year, on April 30, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) called a hurried press conference announcing that he was freezing freight rates to help farmers in their serious difficult time. That time is even more difficult today.
I put a question to the then Minister of Transport. He indicated that the Government would look at it, consider it, but he did not give a clear commitment. The Government did
March 23, 1987

not really freeze freight rates last year. The then Minister of Transport, who is now the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), simply sent back the recommendation from the Senior Grain Transportation Agency which suggested that the volume of wheat to be shipped last year was something like 3.5 million tonnes. Tie asked the agency to reduce its estimates to around 27 or 29 million tonnes, which it did, to 28.5 million tonnes.
As a result, grain freight rates charged to farmers did not rise last year. Elowever, the volume to be shipped in this current crop year has been increased from 28.5 million tonnes to around 31 million tonnes. All of the surplus funds which were in the tally averaging account of the Department have been used up. We are facing a new crop year on August 1 in which the volume has been estimated at close to 31 million tonnes. The Government has to face the prospect, since the Minister of Transport last year reduced the volume, that there will be a serious short-fall.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary responding on behalf of the Minister of Transport this evening will indicate that the Government will maintain the freeze on western freight rates charged to farmers in the new crop year and that the Government will not increase rates by 50 per cent, as has been forecast by the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. If we have an increase of the magnitude of about $3 a tonne, western farmers will be looking at an additional transportation cost of some $90 million to $100 million. This is absolutely unacceptable in the light of reduced grain prices in the new crop year and all the other difficulties facing the western grain industry.
In addition, the Government has not acted on a recommendation of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee which would increase the amount of funds in the Crow benefit by some $25 million, original amount in the Crow benefit was $658 million. The Canadian National Railways has indicated that it should be providing an extra $25 million. That recommendation came to the Department last September-October but still no action has been taken. I hope that tonight the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that the Government is increasing the Crow benefit by some $25 million as recommended by the CNR and by the Senior Grain Transportation Committee from $658 million to $583 million. That amount would also assist in alleviating the desperate situation western
Adjournment Debate
grain producers face in the new crop year with the Government indicating that commodity prices for wheat, barley and other western grains will be reduced by some 20 per cent.

subtopic: RAILWAYS-GRAIN FREIGHT RATES. (B) REQUEST FOR RETENTION OF FREEZE ON FREIGHT RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) said on February 16 that it is still too early to know for certain what will be the rail rate for grain which will come into effect next August 1. Under the provisions of the Western Grain Transportation Act, the administrator of the Grain Transportation Agency, the Hon. Jack Horner, has now issued his official tonnage forecast which is
31.8	million tonnes. The Act then requires that the Canadian Transport Commission use this grain forecast to set the new rail rate. The CTC has until April 30 to complete its calculations and issue the new rate.
When the Government came into office, we moved immediately on amendments to the legislation to implement our election promise to establish a ceiling on the shippers' share of the grain freight rates. The passage of Bill C-44 limited the shippers' share to a maximum of $7.70 per tonne until July 1987. Indeed, the producers' actual share of the freight rate was $7.70 per tonne in 1984-85, $6 per tonne in 1985-86 and $5.97 per tonne in 1986-87. As a consequence, over the past two years, the producers' share of the freight rate fell by more than 20 per cent since we came into office. It now represents a relatively small proportion of the producers' total input costs.
The CTC has not yet calculated the freight rate for 1987-88.
I	would remind the Hon. Member of the announcement of a $1 billion assistance program for grain producers made on December 9, 1986. Under the Special Canadian Grains Program, Canada's grain and oilseed farmers will receive cash payments to cushion the impact of the subsidy war between the EEC and the United States. The Government is indeed sensitive to the plight of Canadian grain farmers.
